records.article:
# What does the reported Alberti branch arithmetic establish?

The [Alberti-disk proposal](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=alberti-disk-branches) combines movable alphabets, four rule transitions, a repeating shift sequence and branches at punctuation. Its LP2-39 reading would require **all** of those pieces. The supplied discussion refers to separate method files and diagrams, but the text available for this audit does not fix the complete disk alphabets and transition rules. We therefore tested two narrower claims that can be checked directly: the identified LP2-39 row and the later 4–5–4 shift arithmetic. **This is not a replay of the proposed decryption.**

![Four cards show the source row's 19 runes, the reproducing left and right raw shift totals, and the right totals' different modulo-31 residues.](experiments/records/alberti-branch-arithmetic/summary.svg)

## What matches

The specified second-section row of [LP2-39](#/page/lp2-39) is present in the archived transcription. It has **19 runes** in five pieces of **3, 4, 6, 5 and 1**, separated by one full stop and three hyphens. The discussion represents these boundaries with other marks in its display; the rune groups are the same. The marks can define *candidate* branch points, but their presence does not tell us what disk state to inherit or which branches to read.

The source also supplies thirteen signed numbers for each of two plant readings, a four-number overlay `−5, −6, −3, −11`, and final arrays split into groups of 4, 5 and 4. All four **raw short-group sums** reproduce:

| Sequence | First four plus overlay | Last four plus overlay | Posted raw totals |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Left | −13 | −17 | −13, −17 |
| Right | −33 | −39 | −33, −39 |

The posted final arrays also total **−13, −15, −17** on the left and **−33, −15, −39** on the right. The middle-group −15 is therefore an arithmetic property of those supplied arrays. It does not independently verify that the plant was counted correctly, that the grouping was fixed before the matching words were selected, or that these shifts decode a page.

## The modulo sign matters

The source next writes the right short totals as `−33 ≡ +2` and `−39 ≡ +8` modulo 31. Under ordinary modulo arithmetic, they are **−2 ≡ 29** and **−8 ≡ 23**. The stated positive **2** and **8** are the *opposite* residues. A mirror operation might deliberately reverse direction, but that would be an additional sign-conversion rule; it does not follow from reduction modulo 31 alone. The source's disk alphabets and direction convention are needed to check that separate step.

As an alignment-sensitivity check, the script also rotates each fixed thirteen-number plant sequence through all **13** starting positions, keeping the same 4–5–4 grouping and overlay. The left ordered raw target `−13, −17` occurs at its posted start only. None of the right rotations gives the posted **positive** residue pair `2, 8` under ordinary modulo 31. These 13 rotations are a limited diagnostic, **not** a random null or a probability of the whole proposal: the source explored other disk sizes, mirror models, shifts, branches and readings.

## What remains untested

The candidate words on LP2-39 are assembled across output branches after disk changes. The text we have does not provide a complete frozen machine-readable transition table, both disk alphabets for every variant, the branch inheritance rule, or a rule for selecting and assembling final letters. We cannot infer those missing rules from an appealing output. In particular, this audit neither confirms nor excludes an Alberti-style cipher, and it does not attach a probability to the reported names or words.

To test the reading, pin one version of the source model, execute **every branch** of this row, save all unedited output and word-selection decisions, and run the same search on solved-page and matched control inputs. The [plan](experiments/records/alberti-branch-arithmetic/plan.json) and [results](experiments/records/alberti-branch-arithmetic/results.json) preserve exactly the narrower checks done here.

From the repository or extracted experiment bundle, run:

```text
python experiments/records/alberti-branch-arithmetic/run.py --check
python experiments/records/alberti-branch-arithmetic/check.py
```

Both scripts use the Python standard library. The checker independently recounts the row, recalculates the posted arrays and residues, and repeats all 26 rotated short-group calculations without importing the producer.

# Cryptographic seed streams against fixed LP2 openings

**Finding.** We generated all **1,385,600** configurations in a published cryptographic-keystream grid and checked whether any can produce one of nine fixed, 12-rune known-reading openings at the start of the **55 nonempty pages in LP2-00–55** (LP2-50 is blank). **None reaches 12 runes.** The longest structurally possible prefix is six. This checks a new, narrow question against the published key candidates; it does not reproduce the source project's original English-scoring sweep.

![Of 1,385,600 configurations, one can match six runes of a fixed opening, but none can match all twelve.](experiments/records/b04-source-seeds-opening-cribs/opening-prefix-funnel.svg)

## What we tested

The [B-04 source dictionary](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round13/B04/seeds.py) provides **2,165 distinct byte seeds**, drawn from puzzle words, numbers, addresses and other source material. The [source generator](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round13/B04/ks.py) expands each seed through 16 byte-stream generators (including hashes, HMAC, RC4, AES-CTR and ChaCha20) and five reductions to the 29-rune alphabet. We kept the source's forward/reversed stream, both decode signs, optional Atbash on the ciphertext, and zero key offset. That is **2,165 × 16 × 5 × 2 × 2 × 2** configurations.

For each configuration we asked a fixed question: could the first 12 ciphertext runes of any included page decode to the first 12 runes of any of nine published readings? The readings were fixed before this run and their source CSV hashes are in the result file. Each page starts a fresh key stream. The solver permits **zero to three rejected key symbols** between emitted runes, exactly the key-skip rule used by the [source decoder](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/campaign18_skip/skipdecode.py). A rejected symbol is allowed only if it would have repeated the preceding ciphertext rune. We checked path existence exactly, without pruning paths by English score. For the reversed-key branch, we generated the full source-length stream before reversing it.

## What happened

| Longest possible prefix | Configurations |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 rune | 890,320 |
| 2 runes | 469,639 |
| 3 runes | 24,653 |
| 4 runes | 950 |
| 5 runes | 37 |
| 6 runes | 1 |
| 12 runes | **0** |

These counts give the *best* prefix across the 55 pages and nine cribs for each configuration. A one-rune match is expected often because there are many possible page-and-crib pairs; the result that matters for this bounded claim is **zero complete 12-rune openings**. This is an exact search over the declared grid, not a statistical estimate of every possible key.

The source B-04 campaign scored candidate plaintext as English on the first 120 runes of LP2-00. Our check changes both the target and the test: it searches page starts across LP2 for **nine specific openings**. Therefore the finding should be read as: *these source-defined zero-offset keystreams do not produce those openings under this structural key-skip rule*. It does not establish that LP2 begins with one of those readings, nor that the entire keystream family has been eliminated. Other plaintexts, offsets, word resets, key-construction changes, and different transcriptions remain outside this record.

## Reproduce and inspect

The bundled seed manifest records the exact ordered source seed bytes. From the repository root, run:

```bash
python experiments/records/b04-source-seeds-opening-cribs/run.py
python experiments/records/b04-source-seeds-opening-cribs/check.py
python experiments/records/b04-source-seeds-opening-cribs/plot.py --check
```

`run.py` emits aggregate counts and a SHA-256 digest of every configuration's best prefix and full-match list; the per-configuration grid is not presented as 1.38 million separate experiments. The independent checker compares the dynamic program with exhaustive skip-path enumeration on 400 random cases and 100 constructed valid skip paths, then verifies planted no-skip and forced-skip positives. The source code copied here retains its MIT license. The experiment uses the site's current page transcription and published reading CSVs; changing those inputs requires a new run.

records.article:
## Finding

If a block operation prevents adjacent repeats *inside* each block but leaves ordinary repeat chances *between* blocks, the few repeats should collect at block boundaries. That concentration is absent for the page-start-anchored sizes raised in prior discussion: **18 of 86** doublets at size 5, **13** at size 7, and **6** at size 13. Conditional on each page's observed doublet count, the expected counts are **17.1**, **12.1**, and **6.4**.

![Observed doublets at size-five, seven and thirteen boundaries compared with controls.](experiments/records/block-boundary-doublets/boundaries.svg)

We also searched sizes 2–29 and every shared offset: **434 placements**. The strongest is size 12, offset 8, with 15 events versus 7.1 expected. But **2,181 of 3,000** matched randomizations produced an equal or stronger best standardized excess somewhere in that same search. Choosing the best-looking size after inspection therefore supplies no evidence for this fixed-boundary model.

## What was counted

For each page, remove non-rune characters and mark every equal pair at neighboring rune positions. The edge from rune position *i* to *i + 1* has phase `(i + 1) mod block size`; phase zero is the ordinary boundary when counting restarts at each page. The run preserves the complete 86-event ledger in its JSON output. It never joins pages or assumes that a slash or hyphen restarts a block.

The control randomly places exactly the observed number of events within each page's available edges. That deliberately conditions on the scarce overall count and asks only whether **placement** has a periodic signature. It does not model language or an encryption process. A cipher with a separate starting phase on each page, variable-size blocks, or interrupted counter could evade this particular test; those rules would need to be fixed and tested separately.

## Reproduce

Python 3.12 and its standard library suffice:

```text
python experiments/records/block-boundary-doublets/run.py --check
python experiments/records/block-boundary-doublets/check.py
```

The first command repeats all 3,000 seeded controls. The second independently recounts the event positions and fixed-size boundary hits. The [machine-readable result](experiments/records/block-boundary-doublets/results.json) records every page's event positions, input hashes, selected-search control, and the three fixed-size comparisons.

records.article:
# A block-start lookahead feedback rule

**Finding.** We made one posted block-feedback formula runnable by fixing its unspecified key to zero and its final lookahead to zero. Blocks of **five** and **seven** round-trip all 15 planted known-reading pages, so the decoder implements the declared rule. On LP2-00–55, neither block size reproduces any of the **15 fixed known 12-rune openings** at the start of any of the **55 nonempty pages** (825 comparisons per size). Its decoded rune distribution remains close to the raw manuscript's flat distribution. This is a result for the stated zero-key completion, not a rejection of the posted idea with an unknown key.

![At a block start, the ciphertext depends on a plaintext rune one block ahead. The decoded LP2 distribution remains close to raw LP2 and far from the solved LP1 reading control.](experiments/records/block-lookahead-feedback/lookahead-feedback.svg)

The source discussion proposed a way for ciphertext feedback to restart at regular boundaries. At ordinary positions, add the previous ciphertext rune; at a block start, add a plaintext rune one block ahead. In zero-based GP-29 indices, our fixed rule is:

```text
if i mod b != 0:  C[i] = P[i] + C[i-1]   (mod 29)
if i mod b == 0:  C[i] = P[i] + P[i+b]   (mod 29)
```

The source's formula also includes a key `k[i]`, but does not specify it. **We set `k[i] = 0` everywhere.** We start a block at each page's first rune, and set `P[i+b] = 0` only when the lookahead falls beyond that page. Those are declared choices needed to run the example, not historical facts about LP2.

## What the test shows

| Stream | Rune count | Index of coincidence | F runes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Raw LP2-00–55 | 12,956 | 0.03448 | 458 |
| Decode with block size 5 | 12,956 | 0.03498 | 171 |
| Decode with block size 7 | 12,956 | 0.03509 | 142 |
| Documented LP1 readings, for context | 2,797 | 0.06114 | 44 |

The solved LP1 sample is a reference for the scale of a known reading, **not** a matched statistical null for every language or every LP2 section. The decoded output's index of coincidence and lack of fixed opening matches give no positive reading under this exact completion. Another key, phase, interruption rule or target plaintext is outside it. The source's reported synthetic size-five run used additional choices and cannot be reproduced from the supplied excerpt alone.

Decoding is direct: subtract the previous ciphertext rune at non-start positions. At the last block start, subtract the declared terminal zero; then work backward through block starts, subtracting the already recovered next block's first plaintext rune. This backward step is what distinguishes this experiment from ordinary lag-one feedback. The [complete report](experiments/records/block-lookahead-feedback/results.json) stores the first 24 decoded indices and a digest of **every full decoded page**, along with each positive-control result.

## Reproduce

The [plan](experiments/records/block-lookahead-feedback/plan.json) pins every LP2 transcription, the known-reading control file, both block sizes, and the missing-rule completions. Run from the repository root or extracted experiment ZIP with Python 3.12 or later:

```text
python experiments/records/block-lookahead-feedback/run.py --check
python experiments/records/block-lookahead-feedback/check.py
python experiments/records/block-lookahead-feedback/plot.py --check
```

The independent checker solves block-start equations as a chain of pair sums and checks all full-page digests. Both implementations recover all 15 known-reading inputs after encoding them. Neither chooses a key or a word after seeing LP2 output.

records.article:
# Replaying the LP2-15–22 Roman matrix proposal

The two supplied guides construct digit grids from Gematria Primus (GP) prime values, map the printed [LP2-15](#/page/lp2-15) number panel into those grids, then connect seven transposed panel entries to Roman numerals and the word **HALFMAN**. We reproduced the stated counts and contacts against Liberpedia’s archived rune text. This is a replay of a **conditional construction**: it has not decrypted LP2-15–22.

![A compact trace from the reported digit grids through the Roman initials, with the local selection check](experiments/records/cc-roman-matrix-replay/trace.svg)

| Check | Reproduced result | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LP2-15 body, excluding nine-rune header | 150 runes → **289 digits = 17²** | The square fit needs the eleven red body runes. |
| LP2-16–22, all runes | 1,744 runes → **3,481 digits = 59²** | A second exact square fit under the stated concatenation. |
| Alternating rune-start/rune-end at 16 registered contacts | **12/16** on 17²; **16/16** on 59² | A real property of the stated registration and streams. The contacts are dependent and the registration was selected during investigation. |
| Transposed panel, positions 5–11, Roman initials | `L X L L L X V` → `L L L L X X V` in direct HALFMAN order | Values sum to **225** and end descending. Ordering does not change the sum. |
| Eight orientations × ten seven-position windows | **2/80** show both 225 and descending output | Both hits use the **same seven panel values**. They are not two independent confirmations. |

## Follow one result

The position map sends printed coordinate 1→2, 2→3, 3→*N*−1, and 4→*N*. On each center-out digit spiral, registered positions 9, 10 and 11 straddle the final inner-square boundary. On the 17² grid, digits 225–226 are the two digits of **X = 47**, followed by the beginning of **NG = 79** at 227. On the 59² grid, digits 3249–3250 are **J = 37**, followed by **Y = 103** at 3251. This reproduces the reported beginning → end → beginning pattern in both streams. The inner-square addresses are fixed by the grid sizes; the rune-boundary coincidence is an additional observation under the chosen registration.

For the number trial, transposed positions 5–11 hold **3152, 3222, 3258, 3278, 3288, 4516, 1206**. Their last two digits are 52, 22, 58, 78, 88, 16 and 06. The first symbols of the corresponding Roman numerals are L, X, L, L, L, X and V. These individual symbol values add to **225**; the conventional Roman numeral for 225 is **CCXXV**, so `LLLLXXV` is an additive symbol list, not standard notation.

The [printed](#/wiki/lp2-15-panel) positions 5–11 have zero-based Fibonacci prime indices **5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89**, which also sum to 225. That arithmetic was already present in the selected panel window; the HALFMAN permutation only rearranges the Roman-symbol list. The proposed words FORK, DEDUCED, ROMANA, TO and HALFMAN come from an alphabet reconstructed from those same proposed word pairs. Fitting them does not independently validate the selector.

## How sensitive is the Roman result?

Keeping the seven-position window at 5–11 but using the printed panel yields **230**, not 225. Moving the transposed selection to positions 6–12 yields **180**. Inverting the HALFMAN order leaves the transposed 5–11 sum at 225 but makes the values **not descending**. Our fixed, local scan checks all eight square symmetries and all ten possible consecutive seven-position windows. Two of the 80 combinations satisfy both conditions, but they select exactly the same seven-number sequence under differently labeled orientations. The scan documents nearby choices; it cannot supply a p-value for the broader search that led to the proposal, which also includes word readings, digit extraction, Roman symbol choice, rank direction and coordinate registration.

The 16/16 larger-grid boundary result is worth preserving as a structural observation. It is not sixteen independent predictions: contacts can share a rune, and the same chosen representation and registration generate every contact. A cipher test would need a rule selected **before** inspecting a fresh passage that predicts where to read, what to emit and how to continue past position 11. The PDFs expressly leave that step open.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, with Python 3 and no external packages:

```text
python experiments/records/cc-roman-matrix-replay/run.py --check
```

The [plan](experiments/records/cc-roman-matrix-replay/plan.json) fixes the source and choices; the [results](experiments/records/cc-roman-matrix-replay/results.json) include every registered address, its rune span, all 80 local Roman trials and input hashes. The [source-intake note](research/source-intake/cc-stage-replay-2026-10-22.md) records the two PDF hashes and scope.

# Do the proposed section sizes form numerical matrices?

**Several proposed areas are exact counts of the archived transcription.** They use different representations: whole runes, decimal digits of Gematria Primus primes, or decimal digits of rune positions. This establishes how those areas were obtained. It does not supply an order for filling or reading a grid, much less decoded text.

| Pages | What is counted | Observed | Proposed arrangement |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| LP2-00–02 | runes | 729 | 27 × 27 |
| LP2-03–07 | GP-prime digits | 2,345 | 35 × 67 |
| LP2-08–14 | runes | 1,729 | 7 × 13 × 19 |
| LP2-15 body | GP-prime digits | 289 | 17 × 17 |
| LP2-16–22 | GP-prime digits | 3,481 | 59 × 59 |
| LP2-27–31 | runes / zero-based index digits | 1,312 / 2,200 | 32 × 41 / 44 × 50 |
| LP2-32 | runes / zero-based index digits | 121 / 196 | 11 × 11 / 14 × 14 |
| LP2-33–39 | runes | 1,680 | 40 × 42 or 7 × 15 × 16 |

For LP2-15, *body* means the rune text after the first nine-rune header line. The complete page has 307 prime digits, so removing that specific header is essential to the 17 × 17 result. The 27 × 27 arrangement has a separate [route replay](#/experiments/totient-map-route), while the 17 × 17 and 59 × 59 streams have a separate [spiral and selector replay](#/experiments/cc-roman-matrix-replay). Those tests are not counted as new decryptions here.

Two other proposals require extra selections. LP2-08–14 gives **2,915** digits with one-based indices; 54 × 54 needs **2,916**. Adding the printed `7` seen on LP2-10 would fill one position, but that digit is not part of the rune stream and its placement is unspecified. LP2-23–26 contains **1,021** runes; 15 × 67 needs **1,005**. Removing 16 runes makes the arithmetic work, but this text-only test cannot identify which runes are red or authorize their exclusion. LP2-33–38 alone has 1,440 runes (36 × 40); LP2-39 has 240 (15 × 16). These component counts are in the [full results](experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/results.json).

## How much does a square count narrow the choice?

![Among 820 contiguous LP2 page intervals, square lengths occur under every tested representation; the figure shows exact counts, not probabilities.](experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/squares.svg)

We also counted **every 820 nonempty contiguous page ranges from LP2-00 through LP2-39** under all four representations. Eleven intervals have a square number of runes, eight a square number of prime digits, three a square number of zero-based index digits, and four a square number of one-based index digits. The proposed 27 × 27 rune interval, 59 × 59 prime-digit interval, and both LP2-32 squares are among them. The LP2-15 body is a different selection, because it starts *inside* a page.

Each full-page target length checked for recurrence occurs once among the 820 intervals *in that particular representation*. The partial-page LP2-15 body is outside this census. This is descriptive, not a uniqueness argument for the method: the targets and section breaks were observed first, intervals overlap, and rectangular lengths have many factor pairs. A compelling cipher proposal would specify the representation, page boundary, any omitted runes, dimensions, start cell and traversal **before** asking whether its reading works on another section.

## Counting rule and scope

We kept only the 29 Gematria Primus runes in the archived LP2-00–39 text files. Headings count unless an exception is stated; spaces, separators, punctuation and printed non-rune digits do not. For digit representations, each rune's unpadded decimal value contributes its own number of digits. For example, a prime value of `109` contributes three cells. The group counts reuse the already pinned [source audit](research/source-intake/cc-matrix-counts.json); the new comparison enumerates every contiguous interval. The checker independently reads the per-page JSON raw transcription, verifies its rune stream against the text file, and recomputes the interval and square counts.

This is one archived transcription, not an independent visual adjudication of disputed runes or ink colors. The proposed grouping, representations and matrix shapes were exploratory. The interval census does not correct for searching other boundaries, rearrangements, partial-page cuts or representations and supplies no chance probability.

To reproduce from the repository root, run `python experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/check.py`. The [plan](experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/plan.json), [results](experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/results.json) and [independent checker](experiments/records/cc-section-representation-census/check.py) give the exact rules and files.

## The model being tested

On each of [LP2-33](#/reader/lp2-33) and [LP2-39](#/reader/lp2-39), label the three horizontal dots A, B and C from left to right. Draw three circles centered at those dots. Can the circles meet at one point on each page if **the same ordered radii** are used on both pages?

The two target points may differ. The radius at A must be the same on both pages, likewise B and C. Both pages remain at their original 2400 × 3600 pixel scale; no resizing or refitting is allowed. This is one precise compass construction, not a general test of compass-related ideas.

**Result: no**, for the measured dot centers at each of the three declared grayscale thresholds. An exact rational distance bound rules out every possible ordered radius triple within this model. It does not require selecting radii from the number square or searching a finite list.

## Measure the centers first

The script reads the original JPEGs, converts RGB to Pillow’s L grayscale, and finds four-connected dark components inside two declared crop boxes. Pixel coordinates are zero-based, with integer coordinates at pixel centers. Crop right and bottom edges are exclusive.

| Page | Crop (left, top, right, bottom) |
| --- | --- |
| LP2-33 | (576, 1656, 1824, 1836) |
| LP2-39 | (1200, 1638, 1800, 1746) |

For each threshold 100, 140 and 180, a pixel is dark if its grayscale value is strictly below the threshold. Retain components with area greater than 200 pixels, width/height strictly between 0.7 and 1.3, and filled area greater than 60% of the bounding rectangle. Exactly three components must survive; otherwise the script stops.

Each center is the arithmetic mean of its component’s pixel coordinates. The report stores integer coordinate sums and areas, so the subsequent calculation uses exact fractions rather than rounded coordinates. This measures a particular thresholded shape; it is not an assertion that the author placed the dot at that exact rational point.

The source-region figure shows decoded original JPEG crops with red center marks. It does not threshold or increase contrast in the displayed image; thresholding is used only to calculate the marked centers. Each crop is fitted to the same display width, so the previews have different scales. The separate spacing diagram uses a common horizontal scale.

At threshold 140, the adjacent center separations on LP2-33 are approximately 417.47 and 478.23 pixels. On LP2-39 they are 196 and 224.5 pixels. The diagram uses one horizontal scale for both pages and separates the rows vertically for readability. It does not show the original vertical positions.

## Why three distances impose a constraint

Let Q be the perpendicular projection of B onto the line through A and C. Write `Q=(1−t)A+tC` and `e=B−Q`. The dots are almost collinear; e measures the middle dot’s small displacement from that line. Let `K=t(1−t)|C−A|²`.

If X is a target point with distances rA, rB and rC from the three dots, expanding the squared distances gives:

```text
rB² − (1−t)rA² − t rC² + K
  = 2 e·(Q−X) + |e|²
```

The right-hand side is an affine function of X. Its minimum and maximum over a rectangle occur at corners, so evaluating the four page corners gives an exact residual interval. No grid sampling of target points is necessary.

Now compare the two pages. Their shared radii cancel except for `(t₂−t₁)(rA²−rC²)`. Each squared radius lies between zero and the squared page diagonal, because both its center and target lie on the page. Consequently:

```text
|residual₂ − residual₁|
  ≥ |K₂ − K₁| − |t₂ − t₁| × (2399² + 3599²)
```

The two corner intervals also give an upper bound on that absolute difference. If the lower bound exceeds the upper bound, no target pair with shared radii can exist.

## The bounds

The table rounds displayed values to two decimal places. Decisions use exact fractions saved in the report; the unit is squared pixels.

| Threshold | Required lower bound | Allowed upper bound | Compatible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | 153,322.33 | 119.47 | No |
| 140 | 155,146.71 | 14.17 | No |
| 180 | 153,854.17 | 11.88 | No |

All three declared threshold variants give the same exclusion. This is a sensitivity check, not a confidence interval or a complete treatment of measurement error. The argument treats each measured center as fixed; it does not quantify every plausible alternative center, crop or dot-selection rule.

## Reproduce

Extract the experiment bundle, then extract the [original-images ZIP](downloads/original-images.zip) into the same folder so that `images/lp2-33.jpg` and `images/lp2-39.jpg` are available. Original images are separate from the small experiment ZIP. Install Pillow 11.3.0 in your Python environment, then verify the required image hashes and run:

```text
python scripts/verify_bundle.py EXPERIMENT-compass-shared-radii-IMAGE-INPUTS.json
python experiments/records/compass-shared-radii/run.py --check
python experiments/records/compass-shared-radii/check.py
```

The producer uses Pillow 11.3.0 and Python’s standard library. Its version is recorded so a different image-decoding environment does not silently claim an exact replay. The checker needs only the standard library. Neither command calls AI or accesses the network.

The producer reruns component measurement, the rational certificate and the annotated source-region SVG. The separate checker verifies source hashes and reconstructs the projection parameter from squared side lengths. It obtains residuals by directly expanding distances to the page corners, without importing the producer. It verifies that identical page geometry is not rejected by the bound. It does **not** independently segment the images or provide a manual review of the dots.

Both checks passed on 20 October 2026. The procedure and controls were recorded in `plan.txt`; the declared thresholds, crops and target rectangle were unchanged after the run. This freshly reconstructs a constrained claim in the supplied research archive; it is not a new discovery. Human review remains pending.

## What remains outside this result

Rescaling one page, using different radii on each page, changing which dots receive which radii, placing a target outside the page, stepping a compass between points, or reading pairwise intersections changes the model. Those alternatives are not excluded here. The result supplies no rune selection or plaintext claim.

For the distinction between an illustration and a specified cipher, see [compass constructions](#/wiki/compass-cipher-tests). For coordinate conventions and original files, see [image regions](#/wiki/image-regions). For how to state this exclusion without overstating it, see [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space).

records.article:
## The question this comparison asks

An earlier word-length analysis compared the unsolved manuscript with thousands of converted texts. Before interpreting a reported rarity, we need to know what was counted, which texts entered the comparison, and whether repeated files received repeated weight.

This experiment asks a specific descriptive question: **where does the reconstructed 2,902-token manuscript summary fall among the first 2,902 tokens of every eligible file in the pinned reference corpus?** It does not ask which language is most likely. The separate [parallel-language experiments](#/experiments/parallel-languages) compare aligned translations under declared representations.

## What the complete audit found

The census covers all **25,906 paths** and **25,844 distinct source blobs**. Of these, **25,565 paths** are long enough for the declared prefix, representing **25,563 distinct eligible blobs**. The other 341 paths are retained as ineligible rows. Every source object and all 46 comparison rows passed the separate checks.

The manuscript has 448 length-two tokens out of 2,902. Only 138 eligible prefixes have a smaller proportion, and one ties it: the inclusive fraction at or below is **139/25,565 (about 0.544%)**. Its 720 length-three tokens give a different position: 24,171 prefixes fall below that proportion, 29 tie it and 1,365 fall above it. These are descriptive counts within this reference collection, not chances that a language or cipher hypothesis is true.

Other measures need not be extreme. The manuscript's variance has 10,995 prefixes below it and 14,570 above it. Its minimum token length of one ties every eligible prefix. Its lack of tokens of length 15 or more is shared by 13,205 prefixes. The complete tables retain these ordinary and tied observations alongside the more unusual proportions.

Removing byte-identical duplication reduces the eligible denominator by only two. For the length-two proportion, the below and equal counts remain 138 and one; the above count changes from 25,426 to 25,424. This sensitivity removes duplicate bytes, not all related works.

## Why 2,902 rather than 2,896?

The [word-length guide](#/wiki/word-lengths?section=historical-count) reconstructs the historical summary by including six isolated digits alongside 2,896 rune tokens. Counting each digit as a length-one token reproduces the earlier summary. This does not make those digits runes, nor prove what the original author's parser intended.

The target for this experiment is that reconstructed historical summary. Switching to the rune-only target would change both the denominator and the reference-prefix length. It belongs in an explicitly declared variant, not an unnoticed correction during the calculation.

## What enters the reference population?

The pinned source tree contains 25,906 paths under `files/`. Every path is considered. A file is eligible when it has at least 2,902 nonempty tokens separated by the literal space character. Its first 2,902 tokens form its profile; later material is not sampled.

There is no language selection, header removal or filtering to the 29-rune alphabet. Strict UTF-8 decoding is required. Token length is the number of retained Unicode code points. A newline or another non-space character remains part of its token under this rule. This precision matters: a general whitespace splitter would implement a different experiment.

The [earlier twelve-prefix audit](#/wiki/word-lengths?section=corpus-inputs) found symbols outside the stored manuscript alphabet. The full census preserves the declared counting rule rather than silently deleting them. Relabeling a symbol one-for-one preserves length; deleting it can change lengths, empty tokens and subsequent prefix selection.

## Two ways to weight the same files

The primary comparison counts every eligible path. If two filenames contain identical bytes, both contribute. This preserves the historical file-based population.

The sensitivity comparison counts each distinct eligible Git blob once. This removes byte-identical duplication. It does not deduplicate editions, translations, differently formatted copies or separate excerpts from the same work. Consequently, neither population should be described as thousands of independent books.

Both versions show the same 23 measures: proportions of lengths 1 through 14 and 15+, mean, sample variance, sample standard deviation, minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum. The 15+ bin retains longer reference tokens even though the manuscript target has none. Measures are related; they are not 23 independent experiments.

## How to read the figure and exact tables

Each bar divides the reference population into values strictly below, equal to and strictly above the manuscript value. “Below” is a numerical relation, not a judgement of which text is more natural or more similar overall. For example, a prefix below the manuscript's length-two proportion simply contains a smaller proportion of length-two tokens.

The tables also retain two inclusive fractions: `(below + equal) / total` and `(above + equal) / total`. Ties enter both. With three reference values below the target, two equal and five above, the fractions are 5/10 and 7/10. They sum to more than one because both include the two ties. Subtracting either fraction from one would give the other *strict* side, not the other inclusive fraction.

Counts, means, variances and interpolated quartiles are compared using exact rational arithmetic. Standard deviation is ranked through variance, because taking a nonnegative square root preserves order and ties. Rounded values displayed to readers do not decide equality.

## What an extreme rank would establish

An extreme rank means that few of these particular file prefixes fall on one side of the manuscript under the specified counting rule. It is not a probability that the plaintext is English, a probability that the manuscript is natural language, or a calibrated hypothesis-test p-value.

The collection is fixed and nonrandom; its edition manifest and conversion procedure remain unavailable. File beginnings can contain material unlike the manuscript. Corpus units count all retained Unicode code points, while the target counts runes plus six digits. These limitations remain even if the arithmetic is reproduced exactly.

For a one-symbol-for-one-symbol cipher with preserved boundaries, plaintext and ciphertext token lengths agree. A mismatch with a reference corpus still does not identify a length-changing cipher: the text's genre, conversion rules, headings and boundary conventions can also differ. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) and [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space).

## Reproduce the comparison

From a Liberpedia checkout or complete reproduction bundle, with an existing local corpus clone and a new output directory:

```text
python experiments/records/corpus-prefix-census/run.py /path/to/project-runeberg --output /path/to/new-corpus-replay
```

Python's standard library and Git are sufficient. The wrapper runs offline and stops when any stage fails. The [reproduction instructions](experiments/records/corpus-prefix-census/README.md) explain source retrieval, each output, and how to resume an interrupted census. The external corpus is not included in the reproduction bundle.

The source checker reads every distinct blob, independently reconstructs the token prefix and statistics, and checks every duplicate row. A second checker independently reconstructs all 46 comparison rows with exact ties. Only after both succeed does the renderer create the figure and tables. These are separate implementations within this project, not an external peer review.

## Sources and scope

The corpus is [mortlach/project-runeberg at revision a39e87e](https://github.com/mortlach/project-runeberg/tree/a39e87ece3e6cbb0f00f7ad5fff9183da5c66d87). The earlier analysis is [mae3301/lp_experiments at revision cb5cdb9](https://github.com/mae3301/lp_experiments/tree/cb5cdb908bb34b68d8a05353eaace56e83d0bbf2). The census and comparison plans retain the counting conventions and input hashes fixed before the complete run.

The [provenance note](experiments/records/corpus-prefix-census/PROVENANCE.md) preserves a frozen test-file hash and documents corruption checks added later. The calculation and audit code match their recorded hashes.

This is a fresh implementation of a declared descriptive comparison. It does not execute the historical scripts, validate their entire statistical analysis, or reproduce an unavailable conversion pipeline.

## Complete corpus comparison

Every planned measure is shown under both weighting rules. Bars partition reference prefixes by whether their value is below, equal to, or above the manuscript value. They do not show probabilities of a language or cipher.

The two inclusive fractions both contain ties: they can sum to more than one. Distinct Git blobs remove byte-identical duplicates only; editions, translations and overlapping works may remain. Manuscript values are exact fractions; length-bin values are proportions. Standard deviation is shown as a square root, while its ranks use exact variance ordering, which preserves all ties.

### Every eligible path

| Length 1 | 89/2902 | 4971 | 192 | 20402 | 5163/25565 | 20594/25565 |

records.article:
# Crib differences as a source-stream search

A proposed approach is to guess a plaintext word, subtract its Gematria Primus indices from the aligned ciphertext indices, and look for that difference sequence elsewhere in *Liber Primus*. This record runs one fixed version of that idea. **Nine exact three-rune matches occur, fewer than the 10.615 mean in 2,000 page-preserving shuffles.** It does not identify a key source or test a decryption.

![Histogram of matching windows across 2,000 within-page shuffles, with the nine observed matches highlighted.](experiments/records/crib-difference-stream-search/matching-windows.svg)

The suggestion was supplied in a 25 September 2026 discussion. It gave no fixed cribs, positions, direction of subtraction or source scope. Those choices here are ours, made for a bounded test. This is **not** a replay of an unpublished result by the poster.

## Rule fixed before the scan

The target is the three red runes opening the lower block of [LP2-39](#/page/lp2-39), with zero-based alphabet indices **27, 5, 15**. We reuse the existing [20-word header-crib list](#/experiments/lp2-39-header-cribs) rather than selecting words after seeing source hits. Exact GP spelling and segmentation leave **17 three-rune candidates**, each producing a distinct difference triplet. For a candidate with plaintext indices P and target indices C, the proposed key triplet is `(C − P) mod 29`. For example, WAY becomes indices 7, 24, 26 under the stored alphabet and gives 20, 10, 18. The [plan](experiments/records/crib-difference-stream-search/plan.json) fixes the entire rule.

Search the other **71 archived text pages**, LP1 and LP2, for an exact forward occurrence of each triplet. Remove punctuation but keep rune order. A three-rune window may cross a printed word or row break within one page; it may not cross a page boundary. No reverse direction, gaps, alphabet rotation, wildcard or prime-value subtraction is allowed. The LP2-39 target page is excluded from its own source search.

| Measure | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Source runes | 15,693 |
| Three-rune crib candidates | 17 |
| Matching source windows | 9 |
| Different candidate triplets with a hit | 9 |
| Control mean, 2,000 within-page shuffles | 10.615 |
| Shuffles with at least nine hits | 1,499 / 2,000 |

The inclusive upper-tail Monte Carlo estimate is `(1499 + 1) / 2001 = 0.7496`. The lower-tail estimate is 0.3833. Neither suggests an unusual excess or deficit of matches under this control. The [complete JSON](experiments/records/crib-difference-stream-search/results.json) lists every candidate spelling, derived triplet, page and zero-based rune offset, plus the complete control histogram. A hit is a sequence coincidence, not a plaintext reading.

## Why the comparison matters

Each shuffled source preserves every page's rune count and length while destroying its original order. The same 17 triplets are searched in every shuffled collection. This accounts for trying the entire fixed crib list, rather than judging whichever single candidate happens to match. It does not model an author's construction process, and it destroys real repeated words and other local structure. The candidate list and three-rune target were already available before this plan, so the result cannot be treated as a prospective test of the broad idea.

A planted positive control inserts the first derived triplet at rune offset zero of the first source page; the scanner recovers it. A separate checker reconstructs source streams from individual stored lines, independently recomputes the GP differences and all observed hits. The producer reruns the seeded shuffles byte for byte.

## Reproduce and extend

Download this record's experiment bundle and run Python 3.12 or later, with no packages or network connection:

```text
python experiments/records/crib-difference-stream-search/run.py --check
python experiments/records/crib-difference-stream-search/check.py
python experiments/records/crib-difference-stream-search/plot.py --check
```

An actual cipher test would need a longer independently chosen crib, a justified key-source location and a rule that predicts **withheld** ciphertext. Searching a longer phrase after seeing these hits, trying both subtraction directions, or allowing interrupted matches creates new search space and needs a new plan and controls. This record leaves those possibilities open; it only tests the rule and source scope above.

# How much can an opening fix in a feedback table?

**Question.** Suppose a cipher has an arbitrary, unknown table with one output for each of the 29 rune indices. If we propose a twelve-rune opening on an LP2 page, how many entries of that table does the opening actually determine?

**Result.** With the previous **ciphertext** rune as feedback, 31 of 495 fixed page-and-opening pairs give internally consistent table assignments. Each fixes only ten or eleven of 29 entries, leaving **29¹⁹ or 29¹⁸** different complete tables. With the previous **plaintext** rune as feedback, just one of 495 pairs is internally consistent; it fixes nine entries and leaves **29²⁰** complete tables. These are algebraic fits to proposed openings, **not decryptions**.

![Nine constrained entries and twenty free entries in one compatible case.](experiments/records/crib-inferred-feedback-table/table-constraints.svg)

## The rule and what an opening can tell us

For each rune after the first, the ciphertext-feedback rule is **Pᵢ = Cᵢ − f(Cᵢ₋₁) mod 29**. The plaintext-feedback variant uses **f(Pᵢ₋₁)** instead. Once a proposed plaintext is supplied, each position makes one demand of the form “table entry *x* must equal *y*.” Repeated demands on the same input must agree. A contradiction rejects that exact opening under that exact rule; a consistent set of *r* inputs leaves **29^(29−r)** ways to fill the remaining table. The first proposed plaintext rune needs an external primer or rule and supplies no table constraint here.

To see whether a compatible opening carries information beyond itself, we inspected the **next twelve ciphertext positions** without using any proposed continuation. For the 31 consistent ciphertext-feedback pairs, only **two, four, or five** of those twelve positions have a previously assigned table input; the rest need free entries. The sole consistent plaintext-feedback pair predicts one next symbol before its next table input is undefined. These are counts of determined positions, not checks against a known later plaintext. No continuation is presented as a reading.

## Scope and checks

The census uses the first 24 runes, including headings, of **LP2-00–55 except runeless LP2-50**, and the same nine fixed twelve-rune openings used in the earlier opening tests. Each page is treated separately, with canonical Gematria Primus indices modulo 29. It does not choose a primer, score English, test other openings, or claim the manuscript uses either feedback rule.

Run `python experiments/records/crib-inferred-feedback-table/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/crib-inferred-feedback-table/check.py` from the repository root. The independent checker reads page JSON instead of the text input used by the producer, reconstructs the constraints with value sets, checks all 990 cases and their forward-coverage counts, and confirms the table-count theorem by enumerating **all 27 functions over F₃ and 3,125 functions over F₅** in planted and adversarial controls. `results.json` retains the case-by-case scope, conflicts, assigned entries, compatible-table count, and forward coverage.

# What does the 729 ÷ rune-index proposal actually produce?

A [reported approach to LP2-00–02](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=cross-section-inversion-729) starts from the section's 729 runes. For each rune, it divides 729 by that rune's zero-based Gematria Primus alphabet index, reduces the integer part modulo 29, then moves by the current line number according to the fractional part. The original discussion also allows neighboring letters, rearrangement and removal when interpreting the result.

This audit checks the **arithmetic and input conventions**, not a candidate reading. The 729-rune total is correct: the three archived pages contain 262, 266 and 201 runes. They occupy **33 printed rune rows** (12, 12 and 9); the number 27 is an arithmetic factor of 729, not the count of printed rows in this transcription.

## The posted first word

The first word on [LP2-00](#/reader/lp2-00) is `ᛋᚻᛖᚩᚷᛗᛡᚠ`. Its GP prime values match all eight numbers quoted in the discussion. The first six zero-based indices also match. For the seventh rune, however, the report treats prime **107** as index **28**; it is at index **27** in the same zero-based 29-rune table that puts prime 53 at index 15. The last rune is F at index zero, making `729 ÷ 0` undefined.

![Eight columns compare the worked example's claimed rune indices with the canonical GP indices and literal outputs.](experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/first-word-trace.svg)

[Open the first-word diagram at full size](experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/first-word-trace.svg). The independent checker verifies the eight indices against a separately generated prime list. The first seven literal outputs, when the posted less-than-half rule includes an exact zero fractional part, are `L O J I C/K H Y`; the eighth has no output. The report's `AE` at position seven comes from its index-28 calculation, not from the archived rune's GP index. This does not identify why the report used 28.

## Complete arithmetic trace

The [plan](experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/plan.json) fixes a transparent convention for a full trace: for nonzero index `j`, compute `q = floor(729/j)`, `r = 729 mod j`, and `base = q mod 29`. Move `+line` if `2r > j`, `−line` if `2r < j`, and zero if equal. Both a global line counter and a counter reset on each page are reported. We save the unwrapped candidate index **and** its modulo-29 form because the discussion does not define how out-of-range positions wrap. F remains undefined rather than being silently changed or omitted.

| Check | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Runes in LP2-00–02 | 729 |
| Printed rune rows | 33 |
| F runes requiring division by zero | 34 |
| Non-F positions with an out-of-range raw index, global line count | 335 of 695 |
| Same, page-reset line count | 124 of 695 |
| Positions where wrapped global and page-reset outputs differ | 396 of 695 |

These last three counts show how much a complete output depends on two conventions the original post does not settle. They are not chance probabilities or language scores. The [complete results](experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/results.json) give all 729 source positions, prime values, quotient/remainder pairs, line numbers, raw candidates and wrapped candidates. No words are moved or deleted in that trace.

## Reproduce and scope

From a checkout or the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/cross-section-index-inversion.zip), run:

```text
python experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/run.py --check
python experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/check.py
python experiments/records/cross-section-index-inversion/plot.py --check
```

The producer verifies the three archived transcription hashes. The checker independently walks every rune, generates the first 29 primes, uses exact fractions to verify the threshold and checks both line conventions. The source discussion is identified by hash in the [reported-attempt entry](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=cross-section-inversion-729); its pasted text is not redistributed.

**The worked first word is not reproduced by one consistent zero-based GP index rule**, and the formula leaves 34 runes without a result. The proposal could be completed by declaring an F rule, one line clock, one wrap rule and one fixed letter choice, but those would be additional hypotheses. A complete decryption claim would then need continuous output, intact punctuation and word order, and a test on text not used to choose the rules. This audit does not exclude every 729-based or geometric approach.

# Do the two preserved LP2 transcriptions change the word-length census?

**No, under Liberpedia's published rune-token rule.** The archived seventh-onion text and the wiki text have **33 different non-rune gaps across LP2-00–55**, on 24 pages. Substituting each gap into the wiki text **one at a time** changes no token-start position. Substituting the complete seventh-onion text also leaves the **2,896-token count, full length histogram, 109 tokens of length ten or more, and the one 11–11–10 window unchanged**. Both texts contain the same **12,956 ordered runes**.

![Cross-source non-rune differences by LP2 page and their token-boundary effects](experiments/records/cross-source-word-boundaries/boundary-effects.svg)

## Inputs and exact boundary rule

The [two-source transcription audit](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions) reports 36 different non-rune gaps across all **58** LP2 pages. This experiment covers the 33 on **LP2-00–55**, the corpus of the published [word-length census](#/wiki/word-lengths). The other three are on LP2-56 and 57 and are outside this comparison. The inputs are the preserved combined seventh-onion text, the 56 wiki page text files and the stored 29-rune alphabet. Every file is pinned by SHA-256 in the [plan](experiments/records/cross-source-word-boundaries/plan.json).

For each source, remove slash row markers and CR/LF wraps, concatenate pages in order, retain headings and all other characters, and match maximal rune runs with optional internal apostrophes. Count runes, not characters in their Latin labels. A token start is the zero-based ordinal of its first rune in the concatenated stream. Neither transcription is declared the correct image reading; this is a source-choice sensitivity test.

| Measure | Wiki text | Seventh-onion text |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ordered runes | 12,956 | 12,956, same order |
| Rune tokens | 2,896 | 2,896 |
| One-rune tokens | 83 | 83 |
| Two-rune tokens | 448 | 448 |
| Three-rune tokens | 720 | 720 |
| Tokens of at least ten runes | 109 | 109 |
| 11–11–10 windows | 1 | 1 |
| Token starts moved | — | 0 |

The [complete result](experiments/records/cross-source-word-boundaries/results.json) lists all 33 differing gaps, their page and rune ordinal, both exact source strings, and the effect of replacing only that gap. Every one-gap variant also retains all token starts and the full histogram. This is stronger than checking aggregate counts alone: two different segmentations could accidentally have the same histogram, but here the start positions themselves agree.

## Why a visible mark can differ without changing this count

On LP2-08, a period in the seventh-onion text corresponds to a hyphen in the wiki text. Both marks separate rune runs under this tokenizer. Other differences include quotes near a rune, number-panel formatting, and terminal marks. They can be important for a rule that distinguishes a period from a hyphen, resets a key at a quote, consumes printed digits, or traverses the alphanumeric grid. This experiment does **not** test those rules. The known five grid-cell disagreements separately alter conditional base-60 bytes; the stable rune-token histogram does not settle them.

Likewise, agreement between two transcriptions does not prove that every mark on the photographed pages was copied correctly. The [page-edge sensitivity experiment](#/experiments/page-join-sensitivity) tests a different uncertainty: whether **32 rune-to-rune page edges** are joined or separated. Those edges change the token count under the same tokenizer. The present cross-source test says only that these two preserved text sources happen to make the **same** choices at every token start under this rule.

## Reproduce

From the repository root or extracted [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/cross-source-word-boundaries.zip), with Python 3 standard library:

```text
python experiments/records/cross-source-word-boundaries/run.py --check
python experiments/records/cross-source-word-boundaries/check.py
```

The producer verifies all input hashes, reconstructs the 33 gap changes, tests each hybrid transcription, and checks the JSON and figure. The independent checker splits the combined source by page, extracts gaps and rune symbols with a separate parser, and scans token starts character by character. Neither script performs a new visual reading of the manuscript images.

records.article:
## Finding

The proposed cumulative rule has no adjustable key: it turns into a difference between neighboring ciphertext runes. Applied separately to every nonempty page of LP2-00–55, its **12,956 output runes remain nearly flat**. Their index of coincidence is **0.035319**, close to the raw LP2 stream's **0.034478** and far below the **0.061139** measured from the site's 2,797 decoded LP1 runes. That comparison does not prove LP2 uses English or the same spelling conventions as LP1, but it supplies no positive reading under the literal rule.

![F-rune rates for the literal output, solved LP1 readings and raw LP2 ciphertext.](experiments/records/cumulative-autokey-literal/f-rate.svg)

The output has **88 F runes (0.68%)**. This number is forced by **86 repeated adjacent ciphertext runes** plus the first rune of each of two pages. The LP1 reading control has **44 F runes among 2,797 (1.57%)**. The chart is descriptive: the corpora differ in length, topic and cipher history.

## Rule tested

The reported formula is `P[k] = C[k] − sum(P[0] ... P[k−1]) mod 29`. We start the sum at zero at the beginning of each page. It follows algebraically that `P[0] = C[0]` and `P[k] = C[k] − C[k−1] mod 29` afterward. The program also re-sums every output prefix and verifies that it reconstructs the exact input rune. This is the literal formula, not a search for primers or a plaintext-feedback Fibonacci recurrence.

## How to reproduce

From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/cumulative-autokey-literal/run.py --check`. The saved [29-value distributions and per-page first-rune ledger](experiments/records/cumulative-autokey-literal/results.json) include hashes for every transcription and reading file used.

This result covers page-local starts and the archived 29-rune transcription. A rule that carries state between pages, skips a rune, adds another key layer, or changes its alphabet is a different test. The known LP1 readings serve only as a transparent comparison, not a formal null distribution for every possible plaintext.

records.article:
# Does the Cypherpunk Manifesto read as an LP2 running key?

**This specific running-key test did not produce a convincing whole-page reading.** We tried every contiguous offset of a pinned copy of Eric Hughes’s *A Cypherpunk’s Manifesto* against [LP2-00](#/reader/lp2-00), [LP2-31](#/reader/lp2-31) and [LP2-54](#/reader/lp2-54). Under both declared ways of turning its letters into key values, each page’s best score was matched or beaten by several fully searched shuffled keys. The same search ranked a planted known reading first under **both** mappings.

![Whole-page scores for two manifesto key mappings on three LP2 pages against fully searched shuffled-key controls](experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/whole-page-scores.svg)

## What was tested

The [source page](https://activism.net/cypherpunk/manifesto.html) is attributed to Eric Hughes and dated 9 March 1993. We preserved the HTML bytes retrieved on 23 October 2026 and used only its essay body, from the first “Privacy is necessary” through “Onward.” The title, signature, address and date were excluded. Uppercasing and retaining A–Z leaves **4,072 letters**. The source URL, raw and normalized hashes, and exact extraction rule are in the [plan](experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/plan.json).

We tested two **different alphabet assumptions**, named in the figure:

- **A–Z shifts:** A=0 through Z=25, one letter per key step. This matches the convention in the [Emerson running-key test](#/experiments/emerson-running-key); it is not itself a GP transcription.
- **GP rune key:** Parse the letters greedily as canonical Gematria Primus Latin labels, including TH, NG and other two-letter labels, with V/K/Z/Q mapped to U/C/S/C. This produces **3,893 key units**. Erasing the source’s spaces permits a two-letter label to cross a former word boundary; another boundary policy is outside this test.

For each mapping and each of the three pages, we tried **every zero-based offset** leaving enough key units to cover the **entire page**. At each rune position we calculated `plaintext = ciphertext − key (mod 29)`, joined the resulting GP Latin labels, and used the pinned English quadgram score. The three page lengths are 262, 269 and 232 runes. The source and the sixteen shuffled copies were searched with exactly the same offsets and score. The shuffles preserve each mapping’s key-value counts; they do not model alternative meaningful books.

## Result and limit

For A–Z shifts, **13, 16 and 13** of the sixteen shuffled-key searches equalled or beat the manifesto’s best whole-page score on LP2-00, 31 and 54. For the GP rune key the counts were **11, 14 and 9**. Those are comparisons of *maxima from complete offset searches*, so a lucky offset is compared with other equally searched opportunities. The figure shows the score and full shuffle range for each case; the [result file](experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/results.json) retains all top-five offsets and decoded strings.

Before examining LP2, we encoded the full 264-rune known reading on LP1-04 using each mapping at offset 3301. In both cases, the identical exhaustive search selected that offset first and recovered the planted reading exactly. This checks the decoder and scorer on a known plaintext. It cannot establish that either mapping is the one used by LP2.

Sixteen shuffled searches give a coarse reference, not a calibrated tail probability. The English scorer can also miss meaningful non-English or unusually rendered plaintext. The result is confined to this archived edition, these two mappings, subtraction direction, page-start clock, three target pages and whole-page English scoring. It does **not** rule out the manifesto under a different rule or running keys in general.

## Reproduce

Download this record’s files and run `python experiments/records/cypherpunk-manifesto-running-key/run.py --check` from the repository root. The independent `check.py` parses the source with a separate HTML parser and recomputes every original and shuffled offset maximum. `plot.py --check` verifies the figure. All three scripts use Python’s standard library and the pinned files; they do not fetch the source again.

records.article: ## The comparison The pale tree on [LP2-55](#/reader/lp2-55) resembles the photograph [DeadTree.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg), credited to R. Neil Marshman / Brookie. This test asks a narrower, checkable question: when the source photograph is scaled and translated over the manuscript tree, does a horizontal reflection fit better than its original orientation? It does **not** seek a decryption rule or recover the original image-editing steps. The published [Commons original](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) is 1,894 × 2,606 pixels. Its local SHA-256 is `608288991f92b8ab901a9fbb39937f93ebdfeb5fd84edeecfa637d5262ff7b29`; its SHA-1 matches the checksum on the [Commons file record](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg). The LP2-55 JPEG is the archived 2,400 × 3,600-pixel page. The script rejects either image if its bytes change. ![Mirrored source, pale manuscript tree and their half-opacity overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-alignment.png) The figure shows the selected mirrored fit at left, the LP2-55 tree region in the middle and a 50% overlay at right. Both source and manuscript are converted to grayscale response maps, enlarged for inspection; this is **not** an unmodified image or a reconstruction of the author’s layer. The source is R. Neil Marshman / Brookie, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), horizontally reflected, cropped, resized, threshold-mapped and blurred here. [Open the original photograph](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) · [Open the unmodified manuscript page](images/lp2-55.jpg). ## Frozen comparison rule The source crop is `[100, 500, 1750, 1950]`; the LP2-55 crop is `[550, 1300, 1850, 2550]`, with right and bottom edges excluded. In each grayscale crop, values darker than the chosen brightness level become a stronger tree response. The source uses `clip((170−L)/130,0,1)` and the manuscript `clip((250−L)/45,0,1)`. Gaussian blur with sigma 7 tolerates differences in stroke width and some missing twigs. Those values were chosen after inspecting the images, so the following scores are descriptive rather than a blind significance test. For each orientation, the script checks 23 scales from 0.370 through 0.700 in increments of 0.015, plus every integer translation that keeps the whole template inside the manuscript crop. The fit score is normalized cross-correlation. In a second run, only the upper 60% of the source template chooses the transform; the lower 40% is scored at that fixed transform. This lower-region check tests whether the upper-branch fit extends further down the same image. It is not a wholly independent holdout because the photograph, crops and processing were selected after viewing both images. | Orientation | Best whole-crop correlation | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at that fit | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Original | 0.377 | 0.564 | −0.095 | | Horizontal reflection | **0.623** | **0.813** | **0.456** | The reflected upper fit uses scale 0.550 and translation `(230,94)` relative to the LP2-55 crop. Its major forks, central branch structure and rightward lower limb overlap in the visualization. The unreflected comparison does not carry its upper fit into the lower region. [Download every scale, coordinate and score](exports/dead-tree-alignment.json). ## What this establishes and what remains open The two declared alignments favor a horizontally reflected source photograph, including the lower region that did not choose the fit. This supports a specific image-source relationship more strongly than a general resemblance between bare trees. The test does not calculate a chance probability against a collection of other tree photographs. It does not establish the exact crop, layer opacity, drawing/filter steps or software used to make LP2-55. Fine branches and the lower trunk differ visibly in the overlay. The [branches guide](#/wiki/branches?section=shared-tree) compares the related treatments on LP2-32 and in the 2016 message. Those carriers are **not** fit by this script. A related experiment now gives each its own crop, response rule and orientation control. Nothing in this image alignment implies a rune operation. ## Reproduce Download the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/dead-tree-alignment.zip) and extract it preserving folders. It contains the [Commons original](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg). Download the [LP2-55 original](images/lp2-55.jpg) separately or extract the original-images ZIP into the same folder. Install Python 3, NumPy and OpenCV (`opencv-python`); the recorded run used OpenCV 5.0.0. Verify the files using the bundled `START-HERE` instructions, then run: ```text python experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/run.py --check ``` To regenerate a report and figure under other settings, edit a **copy** of the script and save separate outputs. Report altered crops, thresholds, blur, scale range and orientation choices. The exact source file, [plan](experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/plan.txt), [script](experiments/records/dead-tree-alignment/run.py), [results](exports/dead-tree-alignment.json) and [visualization](exports/figures/dead-tree-alignment.png) are linked here for inspection.

## One source family, two different treatments

The [LP2-55 source comparison](#/experiments/dead-tree-alignment) favored a horizontally reflected version of R. Neil Marshman’s [DeadTree.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DeadTree.jpg). Two related images remain: a broad, soft tree on [LP2-32](#/reader/lp2-32), and a faint tree behind text in the [2016 message](images/message-2016.jpg). This record measures them separately. The first comparison uses LP2-55 as the reference image; the second returns to the Commons photograph. It does not assume identical blur, brightness or scale across carriers.

The result supports the shared tree artwork under the declared comparisons. It does not recover how the author processed any image, prove a decryption step or assign a probability of chance resemblance across other photographs.

## LP2-55 → LP2-32: same orientation

The script compares the tree region of two original 2,400 × 3,600 JPEGs. It maps their differently rendered dark and pale shapes to grayscale responses, blurs with sigma 15 and searches scales 0.650–1.225 in 0.025 steps. It searches every integer translation keeping the source crop fully inside the LP2-32 crop. Both the original LP2-55 orientation and its horizontal reflection are scored.

![LP2-55 tree aligned to LP2-32, with target and overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-manuscript.png)

The displayed panels are contrast-mapped and blurred for this comparison; open the [unmodified LP2-55](images/lp2-55.jpg) and [LP2-32](images/lp2-32.jpg) images to inspect the real artwork. The unchanged orientation aligns the broad top forks and carries more of that alignment into the lower trunk. The figure shows its upper-region fit and a half-opacity overlay, not an original image layer.

| LP2-55 orientation | Whole-region best | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at upper fit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Same | **0.623** | **0.704** | **0.600** |
| Horizontally reflected | 0.483 | 0.514 | 0.353 |

The same-orientation upper fit uses scale 0.900 and translation `(123,186)` inside the LP2-32 crop. This says that the two *manuscript treatments* preserve orientation relative to each other. It does not contradict the preceding experiment, where both were compared with an originally unreflected photograph.

## Commons photograph → 2016: reflected orientation

The 2016 JPEG is only 563 × 569 pixels and puts pale message text over a very dark tree. The script crops the central tree, maps pixel brightness above the black background to a response, and masks pixels brighter than 100 to reduce the white lettering. It uses Gaussian sigma 1.5 and searches 26 scales from 0.065 to 0.140. The source photograph’s original and horizontally reflected orientations are both compared.

![Mirrored Commons tree aligned to the faint 2016 background tree, with target and overlay](exports/figures/dead-tree-message.png)

This figure increases contrast and removes much of the bright text **for inspection only**; it is not the original message. The source photograph is R. Neil Marshman / Brookie, [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/), cropped, mirrored, resized and contrast-mapped here. [Original Commons JPEG](exports/sources/commons/DeadTree.jpg) · [original 2016 message](images/message-2016.jpg).

| Photograph orientation | Whole-region best | Upper 60% fit | Lower 40% at upper fit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Original | 0.566 | 0.644 | 0.442 |
| Horizontal reflection | **0.854** | **0.826** | **0.858** |

The reflected upper fit uses scale 0.089 and translation `(69,29)` within the message crop. The lower region matches at that fixed transform despite not setting the transform in the declared search. The photograph, crop, text mask and response were still chosen after seeing the images, so these correlations are descriptive, **not** a calibrated chance probability.

## Bounds, files and next checks

The [complete result JSON](exports/dead-tree-cross-carrier.json) records both orientations, 24 and 26 scale values, crops, settings, coordinates and scores. This is one family of related source-image comparisons, not a blanket assertion that every tree image was made with the same filter. Fine branches and the amount of visible trunk vary. No source was inferred from manuscript text or rune values.

The lower 40% check is useful but not fully independent: all preprocessing choices and the two target images were selected during exploration. A stronger source-identification test would score a preregistered set of unrelated tree photographs under the same search budget and report the winner and gap. An exact production reconstruction would need to explain the tonal treatment and branch omissions as well as geometry. Those questions remain open.

Place the original LP2-55, LP2-32 and 2016 JPEGs in its `images/` directory, or extract the site’s original-images ZIP there. Install Python 3, NumPy and OpenCV (the recorded run used OpenCV 5.0.0), verify the bundled files and image hashes using the `START-HERE` instructions, then run:


The [plan](experiments/records/dead-tree-cross-carrier/plan.txt) lists every input and preprocessing choice. # Five-digit chain-addition keys

Could a five-digit decimal primer generate the shifts for the beginning of an unsolved page?

## Finding

**None of the 100,000 primers recovered a fixed known opening.** We tested both addition and subtraction against the first 12 runes of all 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages. That is **99 million exact comparisons** with nine preselected known readings, with zero 12-rune matches. The longest shared prefix was **five runes**. Four page/reading/sign combinations admit a primer for those first five runes, but the sixth rune breaks each one. Five chosen digits can fit five chosen shift values; those short fits do not support a decryption.

![A five-digit decimal primer generates later key digits by adjacent-pair addition modulo ten.](experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/primer-clock.svg)

The example starts with `31415`. Its sixth digit is `(3 + 1) mod 10 = 4`; its seventh is `(1 + 4) mod 10 = 5`. The same rule continues. The [American Cryptogram Association's GROMARK sheet](https://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/Gromark.pdf) specifies a five-digit primer and this chain addition, but the complete cipher also uses a mixed alphabet. **This experiment isolates the digit stream** and uses its digits as direct GP29 shifts. It is a newly constructed LP2 baseline, not a replay of a documented historical attempt or a test of full GROMARK.

## What was checked

Every decimal primer from `00000` through `99999`, including leading zeroes, produced 12 key digits. For each page, we reset the stream at the first visible rune, kept the header, and ignored non-rune marks. We computed `plaintext = ciphertext ± digit (mod 29)` and compared with the same nine 12-rune openings used in earlier bounded tests. The [result file](experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/results.json) gives the complete prefix-length histogram for both signs. A synthetic known reading encrypted with primer `31415` is recovered under each sign.

The [plan](experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/plan.json) fixes the primer range, recurrence and criterion. Run `python experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/decimal-chain-opening-cribs/check.py` from the repository root. The checker independently reads page JSON and counts matching prefixes by enumerating all 100,000 streams. Other page positions, unknown openings, nondecimal primers, alternate GP alphabets, interruptions and full GROMARK are outside this result.
