records.article:
# Directional prime paths: a reproduced count claim

This record checks a specific observation about the alphanumeric grids on LP2-49–51. It reproduces **191 occurrences of 46 distinct decimal primes**, with **1033, 2213 and 3301 absent** from a 49-value candidate set. “Supported” refers only to that scoped recount. It does not establish deliberate construction, statistical significance or a hidden message.

The [grid guide](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) shows the source pages and token conventions. The [prime-path guide](#/wiki/grid-prime-paths) explains the path rule and comparison with the published occurrence CSV. The files below preserve every hit and two independent implementations.

## Fixed search rules

Stack the 32 original rows in page order 49, 50, 51, retaining eight columns. Read four consecutive cells in each of eight straight directions. Paths cannot turn or wrap around an edge, but may cross page boundaries. Reverse directions count separately.

Take the first character of each token. Reject any path containing a 4; do not remove the cell and join its neighbors. Interpret the four-position string as a decimal integer, allowing leading zeroes, and retain it if prime. Then record the four suffix characters and, separately, the base-4 interpretation of the digit string.

For example, LP2-49 grid coordinates (row, column) `(7,2) → (6,3) → (5,4) → (4,5)` contain `0G → 0S → 0d → 2U`. The digit string is `0002`, the decimal value is 2, and the suffix extraction is `GSdU`. Retaining the path does not make those suffixes plaintext.

## Complete result

There are 1,364 geometrically valid directed paths. Of these, 306 contain a 4 and are rejected, leaving 1,058 eligible paths. The decimal-prime filter retains 191 occurrences, including 60 with leading zeroes and 40 crossing a page boundary. These counts describe overlapping paths, not independent trials.

There are 256 possible four-position strings over digits 0–3. Their decimal values include 49 primes; 46 occur in the grid. The three missing strings become 79, 167 and 241 respectively when read in base 4. All three conversions are prime, but that is a separate observation: the original filter tests decimal primality. Only 147 of the 191 retained occurrences are prime under both interpretations.

The JSON contains every retained path, its tokens, original page coordinates, direction vector, digit string, suffix extraction and both numerical interpretations. Its frequency table includes all 49 candidate primes, including zero counts. No appealing suffix string was selected as a successful decryption.

## Reproduce

Extract this experiment’s ZIP with its directory structure intact. Python 3.12 and its standard library are sufficient.

```text
python experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/run.py --check
python experiments/records/grid-prime-paths/check.py
```

The producer uses the shared, included `grid_prime_paths.py` helper to enumerate starts and direction vectors from the coordinate-bearing export. Without `--check`, it prints a fresh JSON report.

The independent checker reads the original archived page records, reconstructs their grid tokens, and enumerates pairs of endpoints instead. It uses a sieve to identify primes rather than the producer’s trial division. It checks the complete set of hits, source coordinates, suffixes, base-4 values and frequency table. Agreement checks the implementations against the same archived transcription; it is not an independent visual reading of every glyph.

## Limits and related variants

Changing to a 16×16 layout, prohibiting page crossings, requiring four nonzero-leading decimal digits, searching longer paths, or requiring both bases to be prime changes the test. Keep such experiments in this family with their changed rules and results visible.

A linked [shuffle-control experiment](#/experiments/grid-prime-path-null) now fixes the path rule and compares the *number* of absent prime values with global and within-row first-digit shuffles. Three or more values were absent in about 15% of each control set. This does not assign a confirmatory probability to the particular three names selected after observation. Shuffling entire tokens would preserve different relationships from shuffling only first characters, and this baseline still does not claim that other representations were exhaustively excluded.

Read [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models and selection](#/wiki/null-models) before turning this reproduced pattern into a claim about intention.

# Prime paths with manuscript page boundaries

This variant asks whether the baseline’s exact three-value missing set survives when every four-cell path must stay on a single manuscript page. It does not: **1103 and 3011 become absent as well**. The original absent values, 1033, 2213 and 3301, remain absent.

“Not supported” applies to preserving the same three-value missing set under this change. It does not reject the baseline recount or rule out a cipher.

## The one changed rule

The [baseline](#/experiments/grid-prime-paths) stacks all 32 rows from LP2-49–51 and permits paths to cross the two page joins. This variant keeps the same row order, columns and coordinate system but rejects a path unless all four cells belong to one page.

Everything else stays fixed: four consecutive cells, eight straight directions, no wrapping or turns, reject any path containing a first character of 4, permit leading zeroes, test primality in decimal, and retain the suffix extraction and separate base-4 value. No cells are deleted or moved.

## Results compared with the baseline

| Measurement | Joined-page baseline | Within-page variant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Geometrically valid directed paths | 1,364 | 1,148 |
| Eligible after rejecting digit 4 | 1,058 | 876 |
| Decimal-prime occurrences | 191 | 151 |
| Distinct decimal primes | 46 | 44 |
| Candidate prime values | 49 | 49 |
| Missing values | 1033, 2213, 3301 | 1033, 1103, 2213, 3011, 3301 |

The removed set contains 216 directed paths, of which 182 have no digit 4 and 40 pass the decimal-prime filter. The remaining 151 hits equal exactly the baseline’s within-page subset, including their complete source coordinates and extracted strings. The variant produces no new hits.

## Why 1103 and 3011 disappear together

The baseline has one occurrence of 1103:

```text
LP2-49 row 10, column 8: 1M
              page boundary
LP2-50 row  1, column 8: 15
LP2-50 row  2, column 8: 0Z
LP2-50 row  3, column 8: 3Q

Forward first characters: 1103
Reverse first characters: 3011
```

Reading those same four cells backward produces the sole occurrence of 3011. Forbidding the boundary crossing removes both. These are two directed hits on one undirected path, not independent locations. This illustrates why counting multiple related observations does not automatically multiply the evidence for an interpretation.

## Reproduce

Extract the experiment ZIP with its directory structure intact. No external packages or network access are required.

```text
python experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/run.py --check
python experiments/records/grid-prime-paths-page-boundaries/check.py
```

The producer enumerates starts and direction vectors from the archived grid export. The checker instead rebuilds tokens directly from page records, enumerates endpoint pairs and uses a sieve for primality. Both enforce the same page barrier. The output retains every hit and all 49 candidate frequencies, including zeroes.

## What this comparison establishes

The exact missing set depends on whether page joins are searchable. Neither convention is proved to be the intended one. Since this variant only removes paths, it cannot restore a value already absent from the baseline; continued absence of the original three is therefore not an independent confirmation.

This is a deterministic scope comparison, not a statistical test. A chance model would need to preserve or deliberately change the relevant page structure and account for the exploratory choice of statistic. Further changes to layout, path length, numeral base or allowed directions belong in separately declared variants of this family.

records.article:
# Does the grid use base 59 or base 60?

**Both are valid ways to number the 256 printed pairs, but they require different digit alphabets.** The archived grid transcription uses 59 of the 62 possible case-sensitive letters and digits: `f`, `y` and `z` do not occur. That count does not tell us the radix. A text can use fewer symbols than its alphabet permits.

The reported base-59 script explicitly deletes lowercase `f` from the candidate `0–9 A–Z a–x` alphabet and moves every later lowercase letter down one digit. Under that rule, `x` becomes 58, so base 59 is mathematically valid. Under the ordinary order without that deletion, `x` is digit 59 and **cannot** appear in a base-59 numeral. This is the difference between a custom alphabet and just changing 60 to 59 in a formula.

![Two digit alphabets: deleting an unused f moves g from 42 to 41 and x from 59 to 58.](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/digit-map.svg)

| Interpretation | `x` digit | `4F` value | Largest of 256 values | Fit in a byte? |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Base 59, remove `f` and renumber | 58 | 251 | 251 | Yes |
| Base 59, keep ordinary digit numbers | 59 | — | — | Invalid: `x` is out of range |
| Base 60, ordinary digit order | 59 | 255 | 255 | Yes |
| Base 62, ordinary digit order | 59 | 263 | 263 | No: 12 entries exceed 255 |

The **byte condition matters**. If each pair must be exactly one unsigned byte and the ordinary digit order is fixed, the presence of `x` requires a base of at least 60, while `4F` must be at most 255 and therefore requires a base of at most 60. That makes 60 the only base *under those two assumptions*. Deleting `f` changes the digit assignments, so the base-59 proposal falls outside that conditional proof. Dropping the byte condition permits base 62 as a positional representation, though not as one byte per pair.

The two valid byte conversions are materially different: **220 of 256 values change** between custom base 59 and ordinary base 60 on the wiki text. For example, the first pair `3N` is 200 in the custom base-59 scheme and 203 in base 60. The fact that both produce 256 bytes does not identify which, if either, was intended.

## Which transcription was tested?

The pasted discussion includes a full 256-pair list. Its count of **59 observed characters** and **161 distinct pairs** reproduces, but that list differs from the wiki export at five coordinates: LP2-49 (6,6) `1L`/`1l` and (7,3) `0L`/`0l`; LP2-50 (11,6) `0l`/`0I` and (12,5) `2s`/`2S`; LP2-51 (8,7) `3i`/`3I`. These are the already documented [source transcription disagreements](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions?section=grid), not evidence for one base over another. They change the exact byte streams and their hashes under **both** encodings.

The more detailed transforms described later in the discussion are separate proposals. This audit does not replay those scripts, test routes through the grid or infer a plaintext. It fixes the elementary input and alphabet question so those experiments can state what they actually used. The [grid guide](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids) explains the page layout and the conditional byte interpretation.

## Reproduce

Run `python experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/run.py --check` from the repository or extracted experiment bundle. The [script](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/run.py) reads the coordinate-bearing [wiki grid export](exports/alphanumeric-grids.csv) and the [256 quoted tokens](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/source-tokens.txt), applies each declared alphabet and checks the saved [result table](experiments/records/grid-radix-reconciliation/results.json). It uses only the Python standard library. The quoted tokens came from the supplied September 2026 discussion; the original linked script files were not supplied, so this checks the displayed list and code excerpt, not an executable historical repository.

# The zero and capital O characters in the LP2 grids

**The current transcription has 65 digit zeroes and seven capital `O` characters in 70 grid cells.** Two cells contain `00`, so there are 72 round marks in total. The coordinate register below covers every cell written with either character in the 256-entry wiki grid. The source-pixel contact sheets make it practical to inspect the whole set, including cells where the two archived text sources agree.

This is an input audit for [LP2-49–51](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids), not a decoding result. A numeral conversion, bit image, checksum, or path can change if even one of these two shapes is copied incorrectly.

## Inspect the printed forms

Each panel below arranges **unscaled pixel crops** from a pinned original 2400 × 3600 JPEG. The small label gives page, grid row and column; adjacent characters may appear to the left or right of the target cell. Open a panel at full size or consult the complete [LP2-49](#/reader/lp2-49), [LP2-50](#/reader/lp2-50), and [LP2-51](#/reader/lp2-51) images. These are navigation aids for a human review, not OCR output.

![Seventeen LP2-49 grid cells with a zero or capital O, labeled by grid row and column.](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/round-glyphs-lp2-49.png)

![Thirty LP2-50 grid cells with a zero or capital O, labeled by grid row and column.](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/round-glyphs-lp2-50.png)

![Twenty-three LP2-51 grid cells with a zero or capital O, labeled by grid row and column.](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/round-glyphs-lp2-51.png)

In this manual pass, the seven entries transcribed with `O` have the broader, rounder form, while the numerous zeroes are narrower. The strongest nearby comparisons are LP2-50 row 2 (`1O` beside `0u`) and LP2-51 row 6 (`2O` beside `00`). I did not identify a definite conflict with the stored `0`/`O` readings. This is **not** independent human certification of all 72 shapes: the coordinates were selected from the transcription, and other characters mistaken for neither `0` nor `O` would be missed. The [JSON coordinate register](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/results.json) gives every original crop rectangle for further review.

| Page | Grid row, column | Transcribed capital-O entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LP2-49 | 6, 2 | `1O` |
| LP2-49 | 10, 6 | `2O` |
| LP2-50 | 2, 6 | `1O` |
| LP2-50 | 13, 5 | `2O` |
| LP2-51 | 4, 8 | `1O` |
| LP2-51 | 6, 5 | `2O` |
| LP2-51 | 8, 1 | `2O` |

The separate seventh-onion and wiki transcriptions differ at [five grid cells](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions?section=grid), but none is a `0`/`O` difference. Their agreement is useful for locating a mark; it is not a second photographic observation.

## What the byte assumption adds—and does not add

Under the [conditional base-60 rule](#/wiki/alphanumeric-grids?section=unique-base), `0` has digit value 0 and `O` has value 24. Sixty of the zeroes are the **first** character of a pair. Replacing one of those with `O` gives a value of at least `24 × 60 = 1,440`, outside a byte. Five zeroes occur as the **second** character: swapping four of them to `O` still fits a byte, while `40 → 4O` would become 264. All seven printed `O` characters occur second, and swapping any of those to `0` remains byte-valued.

This arithmetic constrains readings **only if** every pair is meant to be one unsigned byte with that digit order. It must not be used as independent proof of the printed letter or the intended encoding. The [direct-byte experiment](#/experiments/grid-direct-bytes) kept the current `0`/`O` readings fixed; its negative result therefore does not cover all conceivable round-glyph changes.

## Reproduce the register

From the repository root, or with the experiment ZIP and the named image files extracted alongside it:

```text
python experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/run.py --check
python experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/check.py
```

The first script verifies source SHA-256 hashes, produces the same three contact sheets, and records the 70 source coordinates and conditional byte alternatives. It needs Python 3 and Pillow; it makes no network or AI calls. The second script independently rebuilds the entire 256-entry grid from the structured page records and checks every coordinate, token and alternate value. Neither script identifies printed glyphs automatically. The [plan](experiments/records/grid-round-glyphs/plan.json) states the inclusion rule and limitations.

# The ten bare stems in the LP2-49–51 grids

**Ten of the 256 grid entries contain a character shaped like a bare vertical stem.** The current wiki text writes that character as either uppercase `I` or lowercase `l`. The preserved page images show no dot or horizontal foot at these positions, so the shape alone does not settle the case. Six of the ten positions agree across the two preserved text transcriptions; agreement does not turn an indistinguishable shape into a verified character.

This is an **input audit**, not a proposed LP2 decryption. It supplies exact coordinates and a bounded sensitivity calculation for readers who convert the two-character entries into bytes. It does not change the published transcription silently.

## Locate the marks

Grid rows begin at the first alphanumeric row on each page, excluding any runic lines. Columns run left to right from 1 to 8. The diagram maps the ten stems and, in tan, the separate `2S`/`2s` transcription disagreement. Select it for the complete SVG, and inspect the [LP2-49](#/reader/lp2-49), [LP2-50](#/reader/lp2-50), and [LP2-51](#/reader/lp2-51) images before choosing a reading.

![Ten bare-stem positions mapped across the three eight-column grids; one separate S/s disagreement is marked.](experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/stem-map.svg)

| Page | Row, column | Seventh-onion text | Wiki text | If `I` | If `l` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| LP2-49 | 1, 3 | `2l` | `2l` | 138 | 167 |
| LP2-49 | 4, 2 | `3I` | `3I` | 198 | 227 |
| LP2-49 | 6, 6 | `1L` | `1l` | 78 | 107 |
| LP2-49 | 7, 3 | `0L` | `0l` | 18 | 47 |
| LP2-50 | 2, 3 | `3I` | `3I` | 198 | 227 |
| LP2-50 | 11, 6 | `0l` | `0I` | 18 | 47 |
| LP2-50 | 12, 8 | `0I` | `0I` | 18 | 47 |
| LP2-50 | 13, 7 | `2l` | `2l` | 138 | 167 |
| LP2-51 | 2, 8 | `0l` | `0l` | 18 | 47 |
| LP2-51 | 8, 7 | `3i` | `3I` | 198 | 227 |

The last two columns use the **conditional** digit order `0–9`, `A–Z`, `a–x` and the rule `byte = 60 × first digit + second digit`. They are not a claim that the manuscript intended base 60 or bytes. Changing `I` to `l` adds 29 to the value at every listed cell, but the number of changed bits depends on the first digit. The [full JSON report](experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/results.json) keeps all coordinates, both values and the bit differences.

The `1L` and `0L` readings in the seventh-onion text would require an uppercase L with a foot; that foot is not visible in these image locations. The `3i` reading would require a dot; none is visible there. These observations constrain the historic transcriptions without deciding between `I` and `l`. At LP2-50 row 12, column 5, the distinct `2s`/`2S` disagreement is **not** a bare-stem case. In a close view, both preserved JPEG versions appear to show uppercase `S`; this remains a visual judgment for human review. The [five-source-difference guide](#/wiki/seventh-onion-transcriptions?section=grid) retains both text readings.

## What changes if the ten cases remain open?

Starting from the wiki's 256 tokens, the script changes **only** these ten second characters. Each may be `I` or `l`, giving `2^10 = 1,024` complete inventories. The other 246 entries, including `2S`, remain fixed. This is a sensitivity envelope, not a claim that all 1,024 combinations are equally plausible. A consistent font or a future source could constrain several together.

| Inventory measure | Current wiki text | Range across 1,024 variants |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Distinct two-character tokens | 161 | 160–163 |
| Set bits in the 256 conditional bytes | 1,017 | 1,006–1,026 |
| Even-valued conditional bytes | 134 | 129–139 |

The widely cited **161 distinct tokens** is therefore a property of one transcription, not an image-settled invariant. A later analysis that depends on exact token equality, a checksum, a bit image, or a route through these cells should specify its readings and rerun under relevant alternatives. This audit does not test any route or candidate plaintext.

## Reproduce and review

From the repository root, use Python 3's standard library. If using the experiment ZIP, also extract [original-images.zip](downloads/original-images.zip) into the same folder before running the scripts; the experiment ZIP names and hashes its required page JPEGs but keeps those large images in the shared download.

```text
python experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/run.py --check
python experiments/records/grid-stem-uncertainty/check.py
```

The first script verifies SHA-256 hashes for the wiki grid export, archived text and both preserved JPEG copies for each page, then enumerates every one of the 1,024 variants. The second rebuilds the 256 entries from the structured page records and independently checks every saved variant and metric. These checks verify the arithmetic and provenance; a person must still inspect the image shapes. The image files are preserved at [wiki LP2-49](images/lp2-49.jpg), [LP2-50](images/lp2-50.jpg), [LP2-51](images/lp2-51.jpg), and the [seventh-onion source collection](#/wiki/2014-seventh-onion?section=download).

The enumeration does **not** cover `0`/`O` or all conceivable glyph ambiguities, changes in numeral base, or the separate `2S`/`2s` choice. It also does not establish that independently changing the ten cases is typographically natural. Its purpose is to prevent a downstream result from being reported as robust merely because two text sources agree at a visually ambiguous stem.

records.article:
# Fixed-size grouped key advance

What if one key rune covers several ciphertext runes before the key advances?

## Finding

**No exact opening match.** We held each of the 43 archived keys for groups of **two, three, four or five runes**, testing every key phase and every possible group-boundary offset. The **4,326 settings** across 55 rune-bearing pages produced **2,141,370 comparisons** with nine fixed, 12-rune known-reading openings. None matched; the longest shared prefix was three runes.

![With groups of three, one key position serves three consecutive ciphertext runes; an offset shifts the boundary.](experiments/records/grouped-key-advance-openings/clock.svg)

The diagram shows the key slots for a group of three. At offset zero, slot 0 serves ciphertext positions 0–2, slot 1 serves 3–5, and so on. Offset one moves that boundary, so position 2 already uses slot 1. We tested all offsets for each group size. Each page restarts the schedule, and plaintext is ciphertext minus the chosen key-rune index modulo 29.

## Scope and reproduction

The 43 keys are pinned in the [public wordlist replay](#/experiments/public-wordlist-vigenere). This is a **new test of fixed group sizes**, not a reproduction of that source's ordinary one-step Vigenère output. It does not cover variable group lengths, other keys, interruptions, word resets or unknown opening readings. Planted plaintext recovers under every group size; an independent checker rebuilds the page starts from page JSON and applies the clock rule separately.

The [manifest](experiments/suites/classical-key-schedules/manifest.json) fixes every size, phase and offset. [Results](experiments/records/grouped-key-advance-openings/results.json) include per-size totals and all-case output digest. From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/grouped-key-advance-openings/run.py --check` and `python experiments/suites/classical-key-schedules/check.py grouped-key-advance-openings`.

records.article:
## Finding

The 2012 closing message places **131 digits on three physical lines** after “P.S.” A proposed reading turns that ragged block by taking columns instead of lines. We replayed the six fixed readings of the digits alone and four more readings that preserve the **five-character “P.S. ” indent**. **None passes the amended 95% printable-pair screen or matches a pinned longer constant.**

![Printable-pair scores for all ten fixed readings of the 2012 P.S. block.](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/readings.svg)

The often-mentioned short strings **“3301” and “1033” do not occur in any of the six bare-block readings**. When the visual indent is preserved, “3301” appears once in one column direction and “1033” once in another. They are separate four-digit matches, not a continuous decoded message. The surrounding pair-decoded text does not meet the screen: the indented readings range from **73.8% to 78.5%** printable, against the **95%** threshold. All ten derived 131-digit integers also have explicit compositeness witnesses; primality was a report-only observation, not a hit condition.

## Why the 95% threshold matters

The source initially borrowed an **80% printable** cutoff from a test of arbitrary bytes. A pair of decimal digits can only be 00–99, and **68 of those 100 values** map to printable ASCII characters. The old cutoff therefore produced **37 route firings in 200 random blocks** in the source's own control, before the real P.S. block was tested. The source raised the threshold to **95%** and repeated its controls before examining the real readings. Our independent run also shows the problem: **61 old-cutoff route firings** across 200 newly generated random blocks, but **zero** at 95%. All **10 planted readable blocks** pass the amended gate.

The five-column indent was added as a disclosed extension **after** the six bare readings returned no hits. It is reasonable to inspect the physical layout, but a newly noticed four-digit match is not a predeclared success. We retain the observed strings as observations and apply the same fixed 95% gate to the extra four routes.

## Exact scope and reproduction

The [pinned signed-message text](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/source/ky_2012-01-final-message.asc) supplies the three digit lines, of lengths **40, 45 and 46**. The source runner refers to a separate local corpus path absent from its pinned checkout; we used the pinned repository's `.asc` copy and verified that its extracted digits exactly match the source's saved results. The test covers only four directions of column reading, the joined lines and their reverse, plus the four indented column readings. It does not test arbitrary widths, rearranged digits, a different numeral encoding or an unknown running key.

From the Liberpedia repository root, run:

```text
python experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/run.py
python experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/check.py
```

The [result](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/results.json) and [source manifest](experiments/records/h03-ps-layout-replay/source-manifest.json) include the exact input provenance. A separate checker reconstructs all ten routes from the physical lines, checks their scores and short-string counts, and compares them with the pinned source result.

records.title: Can missing duplicate runes hide an autokey pattern?
records.question: Can twenty missed adjacent duplicate runes restore the nonzero difference-diagonal unevenness predicted by one ciphertext-autokey rule?
records.reader_question: Could missing repeated runes be hiding an autokey pattern in LP2?
records.summary: For exact adjacent duplicate insertions, all 28 nonzero rune-difference counts are unchanged. Even an artificial 20-count allowance reaches CV 0.066 against the source's 0.40 signal bar.
records.finding: The pinned transcription yields 9,640 within-word pairs, 60 doublets and nonzero difference CV 0.0608. Physical duplicate restoration leaves that CV invariant for any number of insertions. An exact upper bound allowing 20 freely allocated nonzero-diagonal additions is 0.0656; at 40 it is 0.0717. A separate checker confirms every count and the insertion identity for all 29^3 three-rune contexts.
records.limitations: This bounds only exact adjacent-duplicate deletion/restoration and the specified ciphertext-autokey difference statistic. The pinned source omits pride.txt, so its English-corpus planted-control numbers and surrogate null are not exactly replayed; a declared synthetic lumpy control passes instead. The source amended its chi-square clause after its first run; the physical invariance does not depend on that clause. Other feedback rules, correlated multi-rune errors and nearly flat plaintext distributions remain outside scope.
records.next_steps: A proposed alternative must state how it changes nonzero adjacent differences, or specify another feedback equation with a different measurable prediction.

scope.representation: First 55 nonempty '%' segments of the pinned krisyotam_runes.txt, matching source LP2-00–54 labels; within-word adjacent rune indices modulo 29.
scope.procedure: Compute nonzero difference-diagonal counts and CV; insert exact adjacent duplicates algebraically and via exhaustive three-rune contexts. Give an artificial adversary k=0..40 arbitrary additions to the 28 nonzero counts and compute its exact maximal CV. Plant a separate synthetic lumpy ciphertext-autokey versus uniform control.
scope.parameters: 9,640 adjacent pairs, 60 doublets; 28 nonzero diagonals; k=0..40, with the source decision at k=20; CV signal bar 0.40, safe bar 0.30.
scope.exclusions: Source Pride & Prejudice-based control numbers, source surrogate null distribution, plaintext-autokey variants, other feedback equations, off-diagonal transcription errors, and plaintext distributions that are nearly uniform.

review.reviewer: Independent parser, exact allocation bound and exhaustive local insertion check

reproduction.environment: Python 3 standard library; bundled MIT-licensed source files; no network.

visuals.caption: Exact adjacent duplicates cannot change the nonzero difference counts. Even a stronger 20-count allowance stays well below the source's 0.40 signal bar.

records.article:
## Finding

**A missed repeated rune cannot change the 28 nonzero difference counts tested here.** The source asks whether about 20 instances of *haplography*—writing a doubled rune once—could make a ciphertext-autokey pattern disappear from LP2. Restoring one duplicate changes `a → x → b` into `a → x → x → b`. The old `x → b` transition remains; only the new `x → x` transition is added. Its rune difference is zero.

![A duplicate insertion leaves the observed nonzero difference unevenness at 0.061. Even an artificial twenty-count allowance reaches only 0.066, compared with the source threshold of 0.40.](experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/diagonal-bound.svg)

We reconstructed the source's **9,640 within-word adjacent pairs** from its pinned rune transcription and counted **60 equal-rune pairs**. The unevenness (coefficient of variation, or CV) of the 28 *nonzero* difference counts is **0.0608**. Inserting any number of exact adjacent duplicates leaves that number unchanged. This is an algebraic result, not a sampled search over insertion sites.

The source also gave a deliberately stronger, nonphysical adversary permission to add 20 counts to *any* nonzero difference. We independently bounded every such allocation: its largest possible CV is **0.0656**, still far below the source's **0.40** autokey-signal bar. At 40 additions the bound is **0.0717**. Our independent checker reconstructs the page runs by a separate parser, verifies all 41 bounds, and checks the insertion identity for every **29³** three-rune context.

## What the result means

For the specific relation `c[i] = p[i] + c[i−1] + K (mod 29)`, differences between consecutive ciphertext runes mirror plaintext-rune frequencies. A strongly uneven plaintext distribution would therefore produce uneven nonzero differences. Exact deletion or restoration of a duplicated ciphertext rune **cannot hide that particular difference pattern**. This says nothing about other feedback rules, other transcription errors, or a plaintext whose frequencies were already nearly flat.

The original source reports a positive control made from *Pride and Prejudice* rune frequencies, but its checkout does not include the `pride.txt` file that its script loads. We therefore **do not claim to reproduce its reported 0.842 control CV or 0.784 separation**. Our replacement control is explicitly synthetic and lumpy: a planted ciphertext-autokey stream scores **1.316** after 20 merges, while a uniform stream scores **0.050**. It checks that the statistic can distinguish those two constructed cases; it is not a model of every possible natural language.

The source's initially frozen no-error rule included `χ² < 40`. Its later addendum sets that clause aside because the artificial adversary crosses 40 while CV remains low. Our strongest conclusion—the exact physical-insertion invariance—does not depend on either threshold. The nonphysical 20-count comparison is reported against the source's unchanged CV bar, with that rule change visible in the bundled source documents.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, with Python 3 and no additional packages:

```text
python experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/run.py
python experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/check.py
python experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/plot.py
```

The [result data](experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/results.json), [pinned source transcription](experiments/records/haplography-diagonal-bound/source/krisyotam_runes.txt), and the source's original plan, code and report are bundled. The copied source is MIT-licensed. Our result covers the **single-rune duplicate insertion** mechanism and this one ciphertext-autokey diagnostic, not the whole autokey family.

records.article:
# Can numbers left by earlier puzzles act as LP2 keys?

The 2013 telnet puzzle returned a prime list that jumped from **71 to 1229**. The 180 primes between them, a number in the 2012 closing message, and whitespace-count patterns from signed messages are concrete material to try as keys. A published B3 program converted those numbers to rune shifts and tested them against the unsolved manuscript. This record repeats its exact finite search.

## Finding

**None of the 4,032 tested decodes crossed the program's English-score bar.** The strongest scored **−6.757**; the source required a score above **−5.2**. The two runs we deliberately encrypted with one of these same key streams recovered their intended text, including one where an F rune pauses key advancement. Those controls check the arithmetic and F behavior; they do not show that the source's English threshold would detect every genuine LP2 plaintext.

![The nine numeric streams' best English scores all fall below the source's advancement bar.](experiments/records/historical-prime-and-ps-keys/scores.svg)

The horizontal position represents the best score across all pages and settings for each stream. The labels beside the dots are the measured values. A higher number is more English-like under the source's four-letter-pattern model.

## What the search did

The [pinned B3 program](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/corpus/H-branch-recovery/recovered/claude_master-roadmap-libra-qk527u/liber-primus/analysis/campaign7/b3_hints.py) defines **nine** streams: the 2012 P.S. number as individual digits, two-digit groups, or a base-29 integer; all primes from 73 through 1223 and their adjacent differences; and four recorded whitespace-count sequences. It reduces each term modulo 29 and repeats the stream to cover the target. The prime run has **180 values**. Its first differences have **179**.

For each stream it tested each of **55 rune-bearing unsolved segments** separately and their concatenation. It crossed addition/subtraction, Atbash on/off, and two treatments of F: ordinary encrypted rune, or a copied rune that does not consume a key symbol. That is **9 streams × 56 targets × 8 settings = 4,032 decodes**. These are configurations, not independent hypotheses; one target is the union of the others. The original saved file reports only each stream's best score. Our [case ledger](experiments/records/historical-prime-and-ps-keys/cases.jsonl) accounts for every decode and matches the source summary to three decimal places.

The overall winner was the **2013 whitespace sequence** on source segment `p49`, with subtraction, Atbash, and the F interruption rule. Its score remained far below the bar. The 2012 P.S. readings scored no better than **−6.856**; the omitted-prime sequence scored **−6.895**. The complete list is in the figure and [results](experiments/records/historical-prime-and-ps-keys/results.json).

## Why these are called “missing primes”

This is a **telnet-command** observation, not an omission from the 2013 CicadaOS prime-printing script. A preserved [telnet `primes` transcript](https://github.com/neuroretransmit/cicada/blob/ade9a02889ef8acbc8cde8edbfd0a785c369f4c3/2013/004-first-onion/README.md) shows `71 1229` with no intervening values; the archived [`prime_echo` script](https://github.com/cicada-solvers/The-Complete-Cicada3301-Archive/blob/c3127e0e9eb5afbb582d37988d6369fe38429238/2013/additional%20files/Cicada%20OS/cicados/usr_local_bin/prime_echo) explicitly prints 73, 79, and the rest of that run. The telnet transcript is a later preserved copy, not a fresh capture of the original hidden service. It supports the stated sequence but does not authenticate a command still running today.

## What remains open

The result covers the B3 rules, the pinned transcription, and English scored by this model. It does not test page-specific starting offsets, nonrepeating keys, other uses of the prime indices, or a language other than English. The source did not repeat the full 4,032-case selection on null texts, so **−6.757 is a measured best score, not a calibrated probability**. B3 did not use the 2013 onion-cookie hashes, raw PGP packet bytes, or fingerprints as keystreams; those require their own exact byte selection and conversion rule.

## Reproduce

Download the experiment ZIP and run the two commands from a Liberpedia checkout:

```text
python experiments/records/historical-prime-and-ps-keys/check.py
python experiments/records/historical-prime-and-ps-keys/run.py
```

The checker independently rebuilds the nine streams, scores every case from the pinned rune and quadgram files, verifies the source's maxima, and runs two constructed decryptions. The runner executes the unmodified B3 program in a temporary copy and compares its full result JSON with the archived source output. It leaves the saved evidence untouched. The original program and community note are included with the experiment, with their exact file hashes in the [plan](experiments/records/historical-prime-and-ps-keys/plan.json).

records.article:
## Finding

If I and M act as local markers for F interruptions, one simple prediction is that they should occur close to F more often than page composition alone would suggest. Among **458 F runes** on LP2-00–55, **132** have an I or M within two rune positions on either side. Shuffling rune order separately within each page gives a middle 95% range of **96–133**, with **34 of 999** shuffles at or above 132.

![Observed F neighborhoods against page-preserving shuffles.](experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/proximity.svg)

The observed count sits near the upper edge of this particular reference. It is **not evidence of a reset rule**. The proposed I/M pair and proximity radius were chosen after discussion of the manuscript, and the reported stream-skip idea did not specify a distance or direction. Testing other rune pairs, distances and sections would create more chances for a high count.

## Exactly what was counted

For each F, the script looks up to two rune positions before and two after it, staying on the same page. It scores one exposure if any of those positions contains I or M. Punctuation and word breaks are omitted, just as they are in the rune-only stream. The 999 reference trials retain each page's length and exact counts of every rune, including F, I and M, while shuffling their order.

This does not insert or remove F, model skipped key slots, detect doublet avoidance, or decode a message. A proposed stream cipher needs a fixed key generator and a deterministic transition for F, collisions and I/M before its full output can be compared with a held-out page.

## Reproduce

Run `python experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/run.py --check` from the repository root. The [results](experiments/records/im-near-f-markers/results.json) preserve page counts, the shuffle seed and all 999 comparison counts.

records.article:
# Can image-only detection find every rune row?

This fixed detector does not reliably recover individual rune rows across the eight selected page layouts. It proposes 83 image bands; 43 match the 65 manually annotated rune rows under the frozen one-to-one interval rule. This is a segmentation control, not evidence of an omitted line in the archive.

The computation, independent check and visual review are preserved with this experiment. They establish the behavior of this fixed detector on the selected images; they do not certify the transcription.

## What was tested

The source lead is Dukotah/cicada3301 at revision `f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1`, specifically `liber-primus/analysis/transcription/linecrop.py`. Its row-detection helper operates on the image alone; the later command-line mapping uses canonical rows. We implemented the fixed image-only rule separately rather than executing downloaded code.

The protocol and manual image reference were frozen before detector execution. The detector examines the central 22–78% of each image. Pixels darker than grayscale 128 contribute to the horizontal projection. A scanline is active when more than 1% of the examined columns are dark. Contiguous active intervals shorter than 20 pixels are discarded before remaining intervals separated by fewer than 12 pixels are merged. No thresholds were tuned after seeing these results.

A proposal matches a reference interval when their intersection divided by their union is at least 0.5. Maximum-cardinality one-to-one matching prevents a large band from counting as several recovered rows. The result retains all eligible edges, matching alternatives and omission controls.

## Results and overlays

| Page | Reference rune rows | Image proposals | Matched rune rows | Overlay |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| LP2-00 | 12 | 12 | 9 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-00.svg) |
| LP2-03 | 11 | 6 | 4 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-03.svg) |
| LP2-15 | 8 | 11 | 5 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-15.svg) |
| LP2-31 | 12 | 12 | 12 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-31.svg) |
| LP2-39 | 12 | 12 | 9 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-39.svg) |
| LP2-50 | 0 | 13 | Not applicable | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-50.svg) |
| LP2-56 | 5 | 10 | 2 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-56.svg) |
| LP2-57 | 5 | 7 | 2 | [Inspect](experiments/records/image-row-coverage/overlays/lp2-57.svg) |

LP2-50 contains alphanumeric rows in this inventory, not rune rows. It is a non-runic control, not a zero-percent rune-recovery result.

Every overlay preserves the source JPEG beneath the annotations. Orange R brackets identify reference rune rows, gray N brackets identify other text rows, and blue D rectangles identify image-only proposals. Visual inspection classified all 83 proposals: 43 individual rune rows, 24 non-runic text rows, seven bands spanning multiple rune rows, and nine artwork bands. No reference interval was changed after detection. These categories describe visible regions; they do not identify precisely which pixels caused a merge.

The numerical count alone is insufficient: LP2-00 has 12 proposals and 12 reference rune rows, yet only nine match. Artwork and merged rows can conceal each other's count discrepancy.

## Omission controls and limits

Each of the 65 reference rune rows is separately treated as absent from a hypothetical candidate inventory while the image and its proposals remain unchanged. The report records whether that row can or must receive a match across all maximum matchings. These are deterministic coverage checks on shared images, not 65 independent trials or 65 actual transcription errors.

An inventory-only comparison cannot visit a row omitted from that inventory by construction. That comparison illustrates a coverage restriction; it does not reproduce the source repository's classifier or measure its accuracy.

The pages were selected for different layouts, not randomly sampled. The reference intervals are approximate manual body intervals and prior familiarity with pages is disclosed. Human review remains pending. This experiment does not recognize rune identities, audit within-row insertions or deletions, certify all 75 pages, or show that an archive row is missing.

## Reproduce

Extract the reproduction bundle and original-images.zip into the same root, or use the repository. With Python 3 and Pillow 11.3.0, run `python experiments/records/image-row-coverage/run.py --check` from the root. This reproduces the saved results and all eight overlays in a temporary directory and runs the independent check. To retain new output, use `--output row-replay` instead.

For the individual stages, choose output paths that do not exist:

```sh
python scripts/test_image_row_matching.py
python scripts/image_row_coverage.py --output row-results.json
python scripts/check_image_row_coverage.py row-results.json --receipt row-audit.json
python scripts/render_image_row_coverage.py row-results.json row-audit.json --output row-overlays
```

The producer checks the frozen plan, reference and image hashes. The independent checker uses scalar pixel bytes, regular-expression active runs, rational interval arithmetic and exhaustive matching enumeration without importing the producer. Both use Pillow to decode the JPEGs, so decoding is a shared dependency. The matching unit controls exhaust all 512 bipartite graphs with three vertices on each side.

`results.json` is the untouched first-run report; its status describes the state at computation time. `audit.json` supplies the subsequent independent computational check. `overlay-review.json` records the later visual review and hashes of all eight overlays. Do not edit the first report to imply that review occurred before it was produced.

Future variants should change one declared segmentation assumption at a time and retain this baseline. More permissive matching alone is not evidence of better row detection.

## Related explanations

See [transcription checking](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=coverage-limits) for the difference between a recorded correction and complete review, and [search spaces and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for why a result applies only to the declared test.

records.article:
# Instar's high-frequency line and low hum

The archived *Instar Emergence* has a narrow line at **15,645.89 Hz**. It rises **39.72 dB above the nearby median** in a fixed full-track spectrum and remains prominent in all eight nonoverlapping 20-second windows. A separate low-frequency peak appears at **59.22 Hz**, 14.89 dB above its nearby median. These measurements make the reported spectral features inspectable; they do not identify a recording device, geographic location, encoded message, or watermark.

![Two pinned Cicada tracks compared in the 14–17 kHz band](experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/lines.svg)

## What was tested

A discussion of the music described an approximately 15 kHz “CRT hum” and 60 Hz hum in *Instar*. We checked the exact archived `761.mp3` and used the separately preserved *Interconnectedness* recording as a comparison. Both files are pinned by SHA-256 in the downloaded record. The *Interconnectedness* carrier already has a documented OpenPuff branch, so it is a comparison of frequency spectra, **not** a clean “no-hidden-content” control.

We averaged the stereo channels, measured a Hann-windowed Welch spectrum over the complete 44.1 kHz track, and selected the largest bin in two bands fixed from the report: 50–70 Hz and 14–17 kHz. The FFT segment length is 65,536 samples with 50% overlap. Each peak is compared with the median of a local band, excluding 3 Hz around that peak. The same peak frequencies were checked in consecutive 20-second windows.

| Track | Peak in 14–17 kHz | Above nearby spectrum | 20-second windows above 10 dB |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| The Instar Emergence | 15,645.89 Hz | +39.72 dB | 8 of 8 |
| Interconnectedness | 14,497.23 Hz | +8.93 dB | 3 of 13 |

The low band also has prominent peaks in both tracks, though at different frequencies: Instar at 59.22 Hz and Interconnectedness at 69.98 Hz under this rule. “Near 60 Hz” is a useful description of the first measured peak. It is **not** proof of North American mains pickup: instruments, processing and MP3 artifacts are not excluded by a spectral peak alone.

## What this leaves open

The source did not specify a watermark algorithm, payload or detector. A narrow spectral line is a property of the sound file, not an extraction of hidden data. The proposed ~500 Hz time-localized gaps were not tested here; they need a fixed event interval and a defined gap statistic. A later watermark test should pin a detector and decision threshold, then measure false positives on matched audio.

## Reproduce

Download this experiment ZIP and the reference-data bundle, extract both into one folder and run:

```sh
python -m pip install numpy scipy soundfile
python experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/run.py --check
python experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/check.py
```

The first script checks the two MP3 hashes, recomputes the Welch measurements and checks the figure. The independent check uses a single FFT per 20-second window, without Welch, and confirms both Instar peaks persist. The saved [results](experiments/records/instar-narrowband-lines/results.json) include every window score. Decoding may vary in last-place floating-point digits across library versions; the archived output was produced with the versions stated in the record.

# JPEG byte histograms: the four-page split

**Finding:** The reported LP2 split is present in the archived JPEGs. Of 58 files, **54 have `00` as their most frequent byte**. The four exceptions—LP2-00, 04, 24 and 26—have `44` as their mode. Both groups contain one-component and three-component JPEGs, so component count does not explain the split. Nothing in this measurement extracts a hidden message or shows that any file is random.

![LP2 modal bytes crossed with JPEG component counts, with a shorter LP1 comparison.](experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/modes.svg)

The test counts the **stored file bytes**, including headers and compressed data. It does not count visible pixel values or the individual digits in a hexadecimal display. The source called the common group “null” and the exceptions “random”; here those terms are replaced with the exact byte modes. Even on the page with the most zeros, `00` is only 20.1% of the file, not a majority. Byte `44` is hexadecimal for decimal 68 (ASCII `D`), consistent with the source’s display label.

| LP2 most frequent byte | One-component JPEG | Three-component JPEG |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `00` | 22 | 32 |
| `44` | 1 | 3 |

The same fixed rule gives 15 `00`-mode files and two `28`-mode files in the 17 archived LP1 images. Those exceptions are LP1-00 and LP1-02, corresponding to the source’s one-based “Page 1” and “Page 3.” This extends its sixteen-page list to the full local archive; it does not recreate the missing historical histogram screenshots. In all 75 archived files, at least 92.6% of the zero bytes occur **after the first scan header**. This locates the bytes within the stored JPEG stream but does not isolate every later marker or explain how its encoder produced them.

The [fixed re-encoding control](#/experiments/jpeg-modal-reencode-control) tests whether the byte class survives different JPEG settings. The four page numbers alone do not specify a date, a cipher or a payload. For a fuller explanation of the byte-versus-pixel distinction, see the [JPEG distribution guide](#/wiki/jpeg-byte-distribution).

## Reproduce

Download the [original images](#/downloads) alongside this experiment, then run `python experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/run.py --check` from the repository root. The script checks all 75 image hashes and re-counts their byte modes and JPEG frame components using Python's standard library. [The plan](experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/plan.json) fixes the rule; [the results](experiments/records/jpeg-byte-mode-replay/results.json) list every page's checksum, byte length, mode, zero count and component count. The historical [source file repository](https://github.com/rtkd/iddqd/tree/master/liber-primus__images--unsolved) is not pinned to its October 2023 revision, so equality with that exact historical input remains unverified.

# JPEG byte classes after re-encoding

**Finding:** The four LP2 files singled out in the 2023 byte-histogram report have a nonzero most-frequent byte in our archived originals. That four-page grouping **does not survive a fixed JPEG re-encode**. The same decoded page images yield 23 nonzero-mode files at quality 75, 23 at quality 85, and five at quality 95. A file-byte mode is therefore sensitive to JPEG encoding choices; the grouping alone cannot identify a manuscript layer or hidden message.

![Bar chart comparing the number of nonzero-modal-byte LP2 files in originals and three fixed re-encodes.](experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/mode-control.svg)

| File set | Nonzero-mode pages | Original four still nonzero-mode |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Archived originals | 4 of 58 | 4 of 4 |
| Re-encode at quality 75 | 23 of 58 | 1 of 4 |
| Re-encode at quality 85 | 23 of 58 | 1 of 4 |
| Re-encode at quality 95 | 5 of 58 | 0 of 4 |

The original four are **LP2-00, 04, 24 and 26**. At qualities 75 and 85, only LP2-24 retains a nonzero mode. At quality 95, none does. Re-encoding introduces many different nonzero-mode pages at 75 and 85; it does not simply turn every page into a `00`-mode file.

## What was compared

For each of the 58 archived LP2 JPEGs, the script counts all 256 possible *complete-file byte values* and records the unique most frequent one. It then decodes that original and saves it in memory as a new JPEG at each of three specified quality settings, with chroma subsampling disabled and no resizing. The re-encoded files are **derivatives**, never replacements for the original manuscript images. The [existing byte audit](#/wiki/jpeg-byte-distribution) gives the full original histograms and frame-header checks; this test asks whether their four-page class is stable under a change of JPEG representation.

This is a bounded sensitivity control, **not a randomness test**. The quality settings are illustrative and were not sampled from a model of how Cicada made the original files. Re-encoding can change compressed bytes and decoded pixels, so this result neither explains the original file-production process nor rules out steganography. A proposed extraction must specify its target bytes, algorithm and expected output separately.

## Reproduce

Run `python experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/run.py --check` from the repository root with **Pillow 11.3.0**. The [saved report](experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/results.json) lists the SHA-256, byte length and mode of every original and all 174 temporary re-encodes. The [plan](experiments/records/jpeg-modal-reencode-control/plan.json) fixes the measurement and settings. The source claim and its 58-page table are summarized in [Reported attempts](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=jpeg-hex-distribution); the historically linked [image archive](https://github.com/rtkd/iddqd/tree/master/liber-primus__images--unsolved) identifies its earlier image collection, whose 2023 revision has not been pinned.

records.article:
## Why test readings whose language is already known?

A language comparison should be checked on Liber Primus itself, not only on ordinary translated web text. This control uses **all nine documented reading sections, spanning 17 runic pages**. Their English readings are reproduced with the existing fixed cipher parameters before any statistical comparison. The method is not asked to discover their plaintext.

The result is useful precisely because it is imperfect: **the pooled readings rank closest to English in every tested representation, but several individual sections have a different nearest language profile.** A nearest statistical match is not a dependable language label for a short section.

## What was fixed before scoring

The original plan selects every documented section and the pool, includes headings, and uses the same eight FLORES development-language profiles and length-distance definition as the [baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages). Within each section, page text is concatenated in order and slash/newline wraps are removed. Sections remain separate when their token lists are pooled.

We compare the literal Latin rune labels using the three corpus representations: letters, accent-folded letters, and GP-style grouping. We also compare native rune-token lengths with each corpus representation. Expanding a rune label into letters changes the counting unit: TH can be two letters but one rune. GP grouping is still a mechanical orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic conversion.

## An input problem found in the first run

LP2-56's published literal field includes its hexadecimal target. A general letter tokenizer interprets the hash's letter fragments as extra words. The unfiltered field produces **50 apparent tokens**, while the rune-derived prose has **25**. All **38 excluded non-rune alphabetic characters** in this control come from LP2-56. The other eight sections have none under the same rule.

We retained that first report and froze a separate amendment before calculating the amended results. For every section—not just LP2-56—the added comparison constructs Latin labels from the verified decoded rune trace, preserves nonalphabetic delimiters, and replaces any alphabetic source character that is not a GP rune with a separator. This gives a consistently defined rune-derived text profile. The original unfiltered results remain in the download as a diagnostic, not a clean prose-language control. The amendment was made after inspecting the first run and is not described as part of the original predeclared design.

## Reading the results

The chart names the nearest language profile for each known-English section. Every language uses identical styling. Its first column compares rune-derived letter lengths with corpus letter lengths; the next uses GP grouping on those labels; the final compares native rune lengths with the GP-grouped corpus. The raw report also contains the accent-folded and additional unit-comparison results.

- The pool contains **739 native rune tokens** and ranks closest to English in all nine comparisons. It is still much shorter than the 2,896-token unsolved target.
- The second koan has 87 native tokens. Its letter profile ranks closest to English, but its GP-grouped and native-rune profiles rank closest to a different candidate. The established English reading has not changed; the counting model has.
- The final parable has only 20 native tokens. Its nearest profile changes between letter, GP-label, and native-rune representations.
- For LP2-56, removing hash fragments changes the literal-profile result. This illustrates an input-selection effect rather than new evidence about the plaintext language.

These results do not prove that the corpus method is useless. They show what its successful pooled comparison does and does not establish. None of the nine sections is a random draw, the pool reuses them, and the representations reuse the same text. Do not turn these outcomes into an independent-trial accuracy estimate or a posterior probability for the unsolved manuscript.

## Reproduce and inspect

Download this experiment's bundle and extract the folder structure intact. It contains the corpus references, archived traces, source transcriptions, reading parameters, original plan, amendment, diagnostic report, current report and scripts. Python 3 standard library only; no API or network.

```sh
python experiments/records/known-reading-languages/run.py --check
python scripts/check_known_reading_language_control.py experiments/records/known-reading-languages/results.json
```

The replay first reproduces the literal readings exactly against the stored page records. The independent checker reconstructs profiles from the separately archived CSV traces and a regex tokenizer; it checks all **70 profiles and 90 rankings** using exact rational distances, and verifies the excluded-character counts. This is computational review, not human review or a new authentication of the readings.

[Current results](experiments/records/known-reading-languages/results.json) · [Original diagnostic](experiments/records/known-reading-languages/diagnostic-original.json) · [Original plan](experiments/plans/known-reading-language-control.json) · [Amendment](experiments/plans/known-reading-language-control-amendment.json)

See [known readings](#/readings), [word-length conventions](#/wiki/word-lengths), and the [shorter aligned-passage controls](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks). The [equal-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks reference samples of exactly 2,896 tokens. It does not lengthen these known-reading sections or turn them into independent trials. Genre-matched parallel material and per-section unsolved analysis remain separate work.

FLORES translations and this derived account are provided under CC BY-SA 4.0; source attribution is included in the bundle. Manuscript/source provenance remains documented separately in the page records.

records.article:
# Do “big-gap” pages have larger JPEG files?

An earlier comparison named 16 pages with unusually wide line gaps and 15 comparison pages, then claimed a **74 KB** difference in their average JPEG size. The page lists are useful because they let us check the arithmetic without choosing a new sample.

![The original size labels average 582.8 KiB for the reported big-gap pages and 542.9 KiB for the comparison pages, a difference of 39.9 KiB.](experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/file-size-comparison.svg)

## What we found

The 16 printed size labels total **9,325 KiB**, giving the reported mean of **582.8125 KiB**. The 15 comparison labels total **8,143 KiB**. Their mean is **542.8667 KiB**, not the post's **508.9375 KiB**. Correcting that arithmetic reduces the difference from roughly 74 to **39.9458 KiB**. This correction matters even before considering any statistical comparison.

All 31 printed size labels match the corresponding [archived JPEGs](#/downloads) when each byte length is divided by 1,024 and rounded **up** to an integer. Using the precise byte lengths gives a **39.83 KiB** difference. The two group medians are about 564.2 and 529.0 KiB, respectively. The [result file](experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/results.json) lists every one of the 58 LP2 JPEG sizes and its SHA-256 hash, including the 27 pages not chosen in the original comparison.

As a scale check, we repeatedly split these same 31 files into groups of 16 and 15 at random. In 100,000 seeded splits, **17,278** had a mean difference at least as large as the observed one in the same direction. That is a *descriptive reference for these fixed files*, not a probability that the gap observation is false: the original groups were not randomly assigned and were selected after looking at the manuscript.

## What remains untested

The supplied discussion names the pages and reports a typical **109-pixel** large gap, **73-pixel** ordinary gap, and **129-pixel** exception on the parable page. Its original screenshot coordinates are absent from the supplied text. This record therefore accepts the author's page labels **only as labels for the file-size replay**. It does not independently establish which pages have a large gap, which glyphs caused one, or whether the space encodes anything. JPEG size varies with page content and encoding; a size difference alone cannot identify a font or cipher mechanism.

To reproduce, run `python experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/check.py`, and `python experiments/records/large-gap-file-size-replay/plot.py --check` from the repository root. The independent checker recalculates the original sums and checks all 31 file-size labels against the archived originals.

records.article:
# Do marked lines sit above the large gaps?

One report links unusually tall spaces between LP2 rune lines to an apostrophe, quotation mark or numeral on the line **above**. That is more specific than saying the marked pages have unusual spacing somewhere. We aligned text rows with measured image rows on five pages named by the report and one comparison page. The regions were fixed in the [plan](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/plan.json); this is a selected, local check rather than a whole-book survey.

![Six source-guided marked lines are each followed by a 108–110 pixel gap; 28 unmarked lines in the measured regions have 73–75 pixel gaps.](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/mark-gap-alignment.svg)

The six marked lines in the reviewed page text are LP2-04 line 8 (apostrophe), LP2-07 line 1 (quotation mark), LP2-10 line 8 (the numeral 7), LP2-35 line 4 (apostrophe), and LP2-42 lines 3 and 6 (quotation marks). Each has a **108–110-pixel** blank interval directly below it. The other **28** measured gaps on those pages and the LP2-14 comparison are **73–75 pixels**. The same row boxes and widths reproduce at three grayscale thresholds: 100, 160 and 200. [Results](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/results.json) give every line and gap coordinate.

LP2-35 shows why the text version matters. Its original image has a small upright punctuation mark on line 4, and the stored **reviewed** text records an apostrophe there. The archived **raw** text omits it. A literal search of the raw text would therefore find five of the six marked wide-gap lines and classify LP2-35 as an unexplained wide gap. The correction is already documented in the [transcription decisions](#/wiki/transcription-decisions?section=review-lp2-35); this experiment measures its effect on a concrete image/text alignment.

![Original LP2-35 line-four crop showing the narrow upright punctuation mark among the runes.](experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/lp2-35-apostrophe.png)

This alignment is strong **within the six selected regions**, but it does not establish why the extra space appears. The pages and marker lines came from a report proposing the association; they were not sampled blindly. Letter shapes, font fallback or manual layout could produce the same observation without encoding a message. The 129-pixel parable exception and number-panel spacing are outside this test, as are punctuation marks elsewhere in the book.

Reproduce from the repository root with `python experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/check.py`, and `python experiments/records/large-gap-mark-alignment/plot.py --check`. The checker independently reads the archived and reviewed page records and reduces flat grayscale pixel rows.

records.article:
# Measuring the reported large line gaps

A supplied analysis reports **109 blank pixels** in a large gap between rune rows, against **73** in an ordinary gap, with a **129-pixel** exception on the parable page. We measured fixed rune-text regions on two of its listed large-gap pages (LP2-04 and LP2-35), the named exception (LP2-57), and one of its ordinary-gap comparison pages (LP2-14). This is a check of the visible spacing claim, not a whole-book census.

![Gap widths in four fixed page regions; three listed large-gap pages each have one wide gap, while the comparison region does not.](experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/gap-measurements.svg)

The [original LP2-04 image](#/reader/lp2-04) has one **109-pixel** clear gap among eleven measured gaps; the others are **73–75**. [LP2-35](#/reader/lp2-35) has one **110-pixel** gap among eleven, and [LP2-57](#/reader/lp2-57) has the reported **129-pixel** exception among four. The [LP2-14 comparison region](#/reader/lp2-14) has six gaps, all **73–75**. These are counts of wholly blank horizontal pixel rows, not baseline distances. The full [results](experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/results.json) include every ink-row coordinate. Repeating the measurement at grayscale cutoffs 100, 160 and 200 leaves all four gap lists unchanged.

This supports the *existence and scale* of the exceptional spacing on the selected archived images. The one-pixel difference on LP2-35 shows why a single exact width should not be applied to every page. The forum text does not include the original screenshot coordinates, so our rectangles and pixel rule are a declared independent measurement, not a reconstruction of the author's Canva selections.

The reason for the extra space remains open. The selected pages have different content and layouts. This measurement neither verifies the post's full 16-page classification nor shows that punctuation, numbers, a particular font or a cipher caused the gap. It also supplies no bit-reading rule.

Reproduce from the repository root with `python experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/run.py --check`, `python experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/check.py`, and `python experiments/records/large-gap-pixel-replay/plot.py --check`. The second script independently reduces flat pixel rows and compares every box at all three thresholds.

records.article:
# Does omitting F make both later messages prime length?

**Result.** Yes, under the declared Gematria Primus transliteration. The preserved 2016 and 2017 signed-message bodies encode to **177** and **45** rune indices. Each contains four F runes. Removing every F leaves **173** and **41**, both prime. This reproduces the reported counts, but it is an observation about two known messages, not a decoding rule for Liber Primus.

![A compact comparison shows the original 2016 and 2017 message lengths and the lengths after omitting F or W.](experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/omission-counts.svg)

The messages are stored as **Latin-letter text**. This record uses the site's explicit GP encoding: split into letter runs, map V to U, then take each word's unique shortest encoding with the archived rune aliases. It counts the message body before PGP signature armor, including the sign-off and verification text. A different transliteration or a different body boundary could change the count; neither source message contains literal runes to count directly.

To see whether prime lengths are specific to F, the script applies the same one-symbol removal to **each of the 29 GP runes**. Two omissions leave prime lengths in both messages: F gives 173 and 41, while W gives 173 and 43. The full [result](experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/results.json) records all 29 pairs. This is a finite comparison, **not a p-value** for intent: F was already a salient symbol in the puzzle, and these two messages were selected from a larger history.

The [plan](experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/plan.json) fixes the body, encoding and one-symbol comparison. The script reads the preserved signed payloads and verifies their hashes through the existing [message manifest](data/evidence/later-messages.json). From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/later-message-f-omission/run.py --check`. The public [later-messages guide](#/wiki/later-messages) explains source preservation and signature verification. Prime lengths alone do not say which LP2 positions an F should skip, whether a key advances, or what plaintext should follow.

records.title: Do positional runes in LP2 hide a message?
records.question: Do fixed rune positions or line boundaries reveal deliberate ciphertext forcing beyond the effects of physical line layout?
records.reader_question: Do the first runes of lines, or other fixed positions, hide a message?
records.summary: One of 21 position and boundary checks flags line initials against a flat shuffle. Reflowing shuffled text by fitted glyph widths makes that apparent anomaly ordinary; six bounded English reading families and the other checks find no supported message.
records.finding: Independent parsing confirms 12,956 runes on 594 physical lines. The line-initial chi-square is 78.656 against a flat-null mean near 27, but a layout-aware reflow gives p=0.177 in the pinned source and p=0.195 in an independently seeded replay. The other nine position tests and five rejection tests do not clear their gate. Six English-reading families remain below their own best-of-family null maxima; planted controls are recovered. The layout-aware detector has 200/200 power in the two source-planted mechanisms when at least 60% of line initials are forced.
records.limitations: The width model is approximate and the original typesetter is unknown; the external BabelStone font-width correlation reported by the source cannot be verified because the font file is absent from the pinned checkout. The six message families score English under a bounded keyless transform set. Boundary-rejection tests have little power with only four line-crossing doublets. Planted power applies only to the two specified synthetic mechanisms and fixed phrase; weaker or different forcing remains open. Source message-family nulls were repeated with independent per-family seed states, so sampled extrema differ from the archived serial receipt.
records.next_steps: Specify any proposed reading rule, target positions, and language before looking at results; compare it with a null that recomputes line breaks and repeats the full candidate search.

scope.representation: First 55 nonempty percentage-delimited segments of pinned krisyotam_runes.txt; 12,956 rune indices on 594 nonempty slash-delimited physical lines. Hyphen, period, slash and page delimiters retain the source geometry.
scope.procedure: Replay source C-02 Arm A (10 positional histograms), Arm B (six English-scored keyless reading families with within-family best-of-search nulls), Arm C (five position-conditioned repeat/difference checks), the post-hoc width-fit/reflow confound and planted forcing power curve. Independently parse physical lines, verify position and doublet tables, fit widths and reflow with a separate seeded simulation.
scope.parameters: 55 pages; 594 physical lines; 29 runes; source 200,000 Arm A and C null draws per applicable test; source 5,000 layout reflows plus 2,000 independent reflows; six Arm B families and 56,376 source candidate variants; family-specific null replicate counts recorded in replay-armB.json; 200 planted streams per mechanism/fraction and 2,000 synthetic null streams; per-test gate 0.001/21.
scope.exclusions: Other transcripts and page ranges, ornament- or column-defined position sets, language models other than English quadgrams, transforms outside the 232 per-read identity/Atbash/shift/direction/F variants, external font validation, original typesetting software, and any complete LP2 decryption.

review.reviewer: Independent physical-line parser, all ten positional counts and two rejection tables, source replay receipt comparison, width-aware reflow and planted forcing controls
