# Can each rune label a divisor of its position?

**Not with consecutive positions, under the rule tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in LP2-00–55 contains repeated occurrences whose spacing makes a fixed divisor greater than one impossible, regardless of where counting starts. This is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure archive's C11 claim, not an original discovery.

## Define the rule before testing it

Let i be a zero-based rune position within a page. Choose an integer origin N and a fixed stride s. Assign each rune r an integer divisor q[r] greater than one, then require:

```text
q[r] divides N + s*i whenever position i contains r
```

The same rune must keep the same divisor throughout that page. Divisors need not be prime, distinct, or equal to Gematria Primus values. Allowing all integers greater than one makes this test more permissive than an assignment restricted to primes. Each page may use its own origin, stride and assignment.

This is a necessary condition for a direct smallest-factor or largest-factor labeling proposal. It does not test prime-derived keys combined with plaintext or an arbitrary operation that merely uses prime numbers.

## Why the origin cancels

If q divides both N+s*i and N+s*j, it divides their difference s*(j−i). The unknown N disappears. For several occurrences, q must therefore divide the stride multiplied by the gcd of the position gaps.

For unit stride, a gap gcd of 1 would require q to divide 1. That contradicts q > 1. Running the page backwards changes the origin and stride sign, not this obstruction.

A rune appearing only once has no gap constraint. Two occurrences with gap 1 already suffice; otherwise several gaps may be needed. The report records every occurrence and, where available, a three-occurrence gcd-one witness. It uses gcd 0 for an empty set of gaps; that means no restriction from this particular test, not impossibility.

## A witness on LP2-00

F occurs at zero-based rune positions **7, 17 and 58**. Thus a fixed divisor must divide both 10 and 51 under unit stride. Their gcd is 1. This single repeated rune already rules out the model on that page; the report records the other rune labels as well.

These are positions in the filtered rune stream, including the heading. They are not image coordinates, Latin-letter offsets or positions that count punctuation.

## What the full retest covers

The program reads all 56 archived text files LP2-00–55, retains alphabet runes and headings, and starts each page independently. All **55 nonempty streams** have at least one gcd-one rune. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes in this transcription and is skipped; its alphanumeric grid is not converted into runes.

Every page therefore excludes both forward and reverse unit-stride constructions, even when the origin and arbitrary integer divisor labels are chosen independently for that page. This is an exact contradiction under the stated model, not a low probability or a finite search over origins.

## Why arbitrary strides remain different

With a gcd-one witness, the general condition is **q divides s**. It excludes a stride coprime to that rune's divisor. It does not exclude every nonunit stride.

For a concrete counterexample, set N=2, s=2 and q[r]=2 for every rune. Every position N+s*i is even, so every recorded rune passes the divisibility condition on every page. This construction assigns the same divisor to different runes, which the tested necessary condition permits. It supplies no decoding rule and does not identify which rune to emit at a position.

If a proposal requires distinct labels, literal GP primes, or a deterministic factor-selection rule, those extra requirements need separate analysis. The counterexample refutes the broader claim that this divisibility condition alone excludes all strides; it is not a successful cipher.

## Reproduce and independently check

Download the experiment ZIP and keep its folders intact. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no network, AI calls or additional packages are needed.

```text
python experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/run.py --check
python experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/check.py
```

The first program uses distances from each rune's first occurrence. The independent checker reads page JSON and computes the gcd of all pairwise occurrence distances. It also verifies every displayed triple, the stride-two counterexample on all 55 pages, a valid unit-stride control, and 450 small synthetic origin/stride cases.

Both text sources share archival ancestry: agreement is a computation check, not an independent manuscript transcription review. The earlier archive cites a Lean proof; this package provides elementary reasoning and fresh integer checks, without claiming that the Lean development was rerun.

## Limits and reopening conditions

Changing which characters advance the clock, resetting within a page, changing a rune's divisor over time, selecting an irregular sequence of integers, or transforming the factor labels changes the model. Such proposals are not ruled out here. A transcription correction also requires a new run. This result belongs alongside other bounded exclusions, not under a heading claiming that prime-based ciphers are impossible.

# Why the reported 53-digit reverse-add result is a palindrome

## The precise claim

A [prior LP2-15 discussion](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes) reports distances from word-level GP sums to nearby primes. After concatenating a selected sequence of those distances, the author added the 53-character decimal string to its reversal and obtained a 53-digit palindrome. The thread corrected an earlier 46-digit claim to 53 digits.

This experiment checks **that arithmetic and one conditional baseline**. The companion [word-by-word source audit](#/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation) now reconstructs the same section from the archived LP2-15–16 rune text; its complete 57-word sequence differs from the 53 reported digits. This record retains the exact reported string as its input so the historical arithmetic claim remains independently inspectable. The source excerpt is identified in the [structured intake](data/reported-attempts.json) by SHA-256.

## Input and result

```text
  02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111
+ 11112000425022120013162130300351524151211201217111320
= 13423171635233335155677430603477655153333253617132431
```

The addition is correct and the result reads identically in either direction. The first operand's leading zero is retained when constructing the reversal; as an integer it has no value, but dropping it before reversing would define a different operation.

The more informative fact is that **every paired digit sum is at most 7**. No column carries. If a decimal string has digits `d[0] ... d[n−1]`, adding it to its reversal pairs `d[i]` with `d[n−1−i]`. These pair sums are necessarily mirror-symmetric. Whenever all are below ten, and the outer pair is nonzero, the decimal result must be a palindrome. The reported example meets both conditions. Its palindromicity follows from this elementary rule; it does not require a cipher mechanism.

![Fifty-three paired sums from the reported digits mirror around the center and all remain below the decimal carry line of ten.](experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/paired-sums.svg)

## A matched-digit control

The plan fixes 100,000 pseudorandom shuffles of the **same 53 characters**, with Python's `random.Random(3301)` and no restrictions on a leading zero in the shuffled string. Each shuffled string is reversed and added as an integer exactly as above. **50,442 of 100,000** shuffles yield palindromes. In this run, exactly the same 50,442 satisfy the no-carry condition with a nonzero outer pair.

This is a conditional, descriptive control: it preserves the selected digit multiset but not any GP word order. It is not a p-value for the full search that produced the string. That search could choose pages, word boundaries, nearest-prime ties, zero separators, and which examples to present. A null model for the whole idea must include those choices. Randomly shuffling uniform decimal digits would be a different and less relevant comparison, because the reported distances concentrate at small digits (11 zeroes, 18 ones, 11 twos).

## Reproduce

Extract the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add.zip) with folders intact, then run from its root:

```text
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/run.py --check
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/check.py
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/plot.py
```

The first command recomputes the arithmetic and all 100,000 fixed shuffles. The independent checker verifies the 53 column sums, their symmetry, the no-carry proof condition, and the saved control's internal consistency. The plotter regenerates the SVG from `results.json`. All use the Python standard library. `plan.json` specifies the original digits, seed, trial count and post-selection scope; `results.json` preserves the full paired-sum list and control counts.

## What remains open

The [companion audit](#/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation) pins one source-to-digits derivation. Its archived first-section reading has 57 words, compared with 53 reported digits, and also yields a carry-free palindrome. The author's exact transcription or segmentation choices are not preserved in the supplied report. A full cipher test would still need a fixed operation on unsolved text and a comparison that repeats the complete choice of section, grouping and method.

This computational audit was run and checked by Codex on 2026-10-22. Human review of the source grouping and the mathematical interpretation is pending.

records.article:
# Can the reported prime-distance digits be derived from LP2-15–16?

The earlier [reverse-add record](#/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add) checks the arithmetic of a reported 53-digit string. It does not show how each digit came from the manuscript. This source audit makes that missing step explicit: read every word in the same first section, sum its Gematria Primus rune values, and record its distance to the nearest prime.

The archived transcription yields **57 word distances**, while the supplied report lists **53**. The two strings have a minimum digit-edit distance of seven under ordinary insertion, deletion and substitution. That discrepancy matters for reproducing the reported derivation. It does **not** make the reverse-add observation disappear: the complete 57-digit sequence also produces a palindrome on the first addition.

## Frozen reading rule

The input is the archived [LP2-15](#/reader/lp2-15) and [LP2-16](#/reader/lp2-16) rune transcription. We use the two-word heading on LP2-15, then every rune word after its `$` section marker through the word before the next section's `ᛈᚹᚷᚷ` on LP2-16. The first five values agree with the report's “red header” sequence; the first three body words are red on the page image. Printed square numbers are not words in this calculation.

A hyphen or period separates words. A `/` followed by a line break is typographic wrapping, so runes on either side remain one word unless a hyphen intervenes. The page boundary also does not split its continuing word. For each word, sum the first 29 primes in Gematria Primus order and use the *absolute* distance to the closest integer prime. A tie between equidistant primes does not change the distance. The [plan](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/plan.json) pins both text hashes, the rune-to-prime table, the section end marker and the report's 53 digits.

For example, the heading words give `ᚠᚢᛚᛗ → 149 → 0` and `ᚪᛠᚣᛟᚪ → 489 → 2`. The [full token trace](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/results.json) lists all 57 words, their prime sums and nearest-prime distances, so any disputed separator or rune has an exact place to challenge.

## Where the sequences differ

```text
Reported: 02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111   (53 digits)
Archive:  023111712102410211215142515300303126141002122142400021111 (57 digits)
```

![The reported 53 digits aligned with 57 distances independently derived from archived LP2-15–16 words. Ochre columns mark gaps or differing digits.](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/word-distance-alignment.svg)

[Open the alignment at full size](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/word-distance-alignment.svg).

The figure shows **one** minimum alignment: four archive word positions have no partner in the report and three paired digits differ. The minimum edit count is independently checked by dynamic programming. Repeated digits make the precise alignment non-unique, so these positions should not be read as proof of which words the original author skipped or transcribed differently. The reported list and archived source cannot be made identical under the stated rule without additional choices or corrections.

## What happens to the palindrome?

Adding the archive-derived string to its reversal gives:

```text
  023111712102410211215142515300303126141002122142400021111
+ 111120004241221200141621303003515241512112014201217111320
= 134231716343631411356763818303818367653114136343617132431
```

The [independent checker](experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/check.py) verifies the integer sum and each mirrored digit pair. The largest paired sum is eight, so no decimal carry occurs. That is why the 57-digit sum remains a palindrome.

As a conditional baseline, we shuffled the same **57 distance digits** 100,000 times with a fixed seed, reversed and added each shuffle, and obtained **53,845 palindromes**. This preserves the short-digit distribution that makes carry-free addition frequent. It does not reproduce the full historical search over pages, section boundaries and prime-related transformations. The sibling record's 53-digit control gives 50,442 palindromes in 100,000 shuffles of *its* fixed digit multiset. Neither rate is a probability of intentional construction.

## Reproduce and limits

From a full checkout or the [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-word-derivation.zip), run:

```text
python experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/run.py --check
python experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/check.py
python experiments/records/prime-distance-word-derivation/plot.py --check
```

The first command recomputes every word and all 100,000 shuffles. The checker uses a separate word scanner, a different nearest-prime search, direct column arithmetic, a minimum-edit calculation and a second control replay. The supplied discussion is identified by SHA-256 in the [reported-attempt intake](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes); its full pasted transcript is not redistributed. The report may have used a different transcription or unpublished segmentation choices. Image-level verification of every word break and human review are still pending.

This is an **input-derivation audit**, not a decryption of LP2-15–22. A future cipher test would need a fixed way to use these distances on an unsolved passage and evaluate the complete output on text that did not determine the rule.

# Runes at prime and Fibonacci positions

**Question.** If the manuscript's rune positions act as an index, does reading only prime- or Fibonacci-numbered runes reveal English text?

**Result.** The tested extractions did not stand out. The strongest score was from taking prime-numbered runes **afresh on every page**, then pooling the evidence across pages. Its score was **−7.472**. In **201 of 256** shuffled-page trials, the strongest of the same tested methods scored at least as well (global add-one estimate **202/257 ≈ 0.786**). The extracted text does not form a readable passage.

![Prime and Fibonacci extraction scores compared with page-preserving shuffled controls.](experiments/records/prime-fibonacci-position-extraction/selection-scores.svg)

## What we selected

There are **12,956** recorded GP runes on the 55 rune-bearing pages LP2-00–55. Position **1** means the first rune, without advancing for punctuation or page artwork. Prime positions start **2, 3, 5, 7**; unique Fibonacci positions start **1, 2, 3, 5, 8**. We tried each selector twice: restarting at every page, and applying it once after joining the pages in numerical order. This is a fixed four-arm test, not an every-*n* or adjustable-start search.

For page-by-page selection, we scored each page's extracted runes separately and combined the quadgram sums. No four-letter group was allowed to cross a page boundary. Joined selection was scored as one stream. Three arms supplied at least the **100 Latin quadgrams** declared for scoring: page-local primes (2,797 selected runes), joined primes (1,542), and page-local Fibonacci (634). Book-wide Fibonacci selected only **20 runes**, yielding 20 quadgrams, so its score was withheld. Its exact stream remains in `results.json`; this short sample cannot support a negative language finding.

Every control trial shuffled the rune order **inside each complete page once**, keeping each page's rune counts. All four selectors then used those same shuffled pages. We compared the best eligible observed arm with the best eligible arm in each trial, accounting for choosing the most attractive of the three scored variants. The page-local prime score was only **0.025** above its own shuffled median; the other two scored arms were about **0.057 below** theirs. A planted known-reading stream at the selected positions was recovered exactly and scored well above each eligible arm's shuffled median, checking that the extraction and scorer can respond to a real GP-encoded passage.

The outcome is bounded. It tests direct English-like readings at these **one-based, forward** positions under two page-boundary conventions. It does not rule out a second cipher layer, different starting positions, backwards reading, an indexed key rather than direct text, another language, or other ways of treating page divisions. The source catalog lists the idea; it is not evidence that a particular historical attempt used these exact rules.

Run `python experiments/records/prime-fibonacci-position-extraction/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/prime-fibonacci-position-extraction/check.py` from the repository root. Both use Python 3's standard library. The independent check reconstructs pages from the page JSON, computes positions by a separate algorithm, and verifies all 256 shared-control scores. `results.json` preserves every extracted segment, its GP indices and Latin labels, so the precise reading can be inspected without recomputing it.

# The circumference substitutions

A [public failed-attempt record](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/README.md) applies a circumference-inspired rule to each GP rune: use either its alphabet position or its associated prime as the radius, multiply by `2π`, then reduce modulo 29. The README says **round**, but the repository's [index-radius output](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/pages_2piR.txt) and [prime-radius output](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/2%CF%80R/pages_2piR_primes.txt) use **integer truncation** instead. We replay both interpretations so the source discrepancy is visible.

## Finding

![Distinct output runes under index and prime radii with nearest rounding or truncation.](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/mapping-coverage.svg)

On LP2-00–55, the truncated index and prime maps reproduce the first nine runes on all **55 rune-bearing pages** in the pinned public outputs. LP2-50 has no runic line to compare. The README's nearest-rounding rule does not reproduce those outputs. It produces a different symbol map: the index version reaches 25 of 29 possible output runes instead of 26 under truncation. With GP prime values as radii, both rounding choices reach only **18 of 29** output runes, although the actual mappings differ.

Each rule is a fixed one-rune substitution. In the prime-radius version, 11 output symbols are unreachable. This compression makes the rule non-invertible without additional information; it does not by itself establish that the manuscript was encoded by the inverse rule. The source reports no interesting reading, but supplies no scoring threshold or test that would justify a blanket negative conclusion. Our reproducible result is the exact map and the output agreement.

## Method and limits

The [plan](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/plan.json) pins the public revision, source-output hashes, two radius choices and two rounding choices. The [results](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/results.json) contain all four 29-entry maps and hashes of the transformed text for LP2-00–55. The [independent check](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/check.py) uses a separate floor-based calculation, checks every saved output hash, and can compare both source text files when supplied locally. Punctuation, line marks and decimal numbers remain unchanged; only runes are substituted.

This test neither scores candidate English nor searches secondary keys, alternative page groupings, or a reversible decoding scheme. In particular, a numerical motif is not evidence for a cipher merely because it can be applied to every symbol.

## Reproduce

Run `python experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/check.py`. For the source-output comparison, put the two text files named in the [plan](experiments/records/public-circumference-substitutions/plan.json) in one directory and run `check.py --source-directory PATH`. Their SHA-256 values are verified before comparison.

# Do common key-stretching recipes unlock LP2's opening?

A short password might generate a much longer numeric key. This [published screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/KDF/RESULTS.md) tried that possibility on the **first 120 unsolved LP2 runes**. It crossed a fixed list of puzzle-related secrets with familiar password-to-key recipes, then applied each resulting stream through a decoder that can account for skipped key symbols.

## Finding

**None of the 692,064 LP2 decodes passed the source's English-score requirement.** The best scored **−6.259**, while a candidate needed at least **−5.500** to advance. A message deliberately encrypted with one of the tested recipes *did* come back as the top result at **−4.186**. The control shows this particular search can find one of its own planted messages; it does not establish that every possible real encoding would be found.

![The planted message scores above the advancement bar; the strongest LP2 candidate stays below it.](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/scores.svg)

These are English four-letter-pattern scores: higher values are stronger. The strongest LP2 output still does not read as an English continuation. It used the secret `sacrifice`, 100,000 rounds of iterative SHA-256, the secret itself as salt, rejection reduction to rune indices, an Atbash transform, and a reversed key stream. That is the **best measured configuration**, not evidence that any of those choices is a clue.

## What the search actually covered

The code built **534 distinct secret byte strings** from the source's puzzle phrases, solved-page words, numbers, prime sequences and other named artifacts. For each secret it tried **27 key-derivation configurations**: PBKDF2 variants, scrypt, iterated hashes and OpenSSL-style derivation. It then crossed three salts (`empty`, `3301`, and the secret itself), two byte-to-rune reductions, both arithmetic signs, Atbash on or off, and forward or reversed key output. All began at **key offset zero** and were scored against the same 120-rune LP2 prefix.

The source first ran two controls. One recovered a message from a short-seed SHA-256 expander with **98.9%** character agreement; the other planted a PBKDF2 message and searched the *entire same configuration grid* against it, ranking the planted setting first. The latter required another 692,064 control decodes. Those are a power check, not another 692,064 distinct LP2 hypotheses.

The source's 200 shuffled-text comparisons use one fixed control key. They do **not** rerun the full 692,064-choice search on each shuffle, so they do not provide a calibrated probability for the winning LP2 score after selection. The finding here is narrower and cleaner: the executed grid, with its stated English threshold, produced no advancing LP2 result.

This does not test a different secret, salt, iteration count, starting offset, language, changing key by page, or a longer portion of LP2. It says nothing about whether LP2 could use a key-stretching recipe outside this specific grid.

## Reproduce

Download the record's ZIP to inspect the pinned code and inputs. The bundled subset is byte-for-byte source code and the input files that affect this run; its rebuilt **ordered 534-secret dictionary matches the full source checkout by SHA-256**. From a Liberpedia repository checkout:

```bash
python experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/check.py
python experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/run.py
```

The checker quickly verifies the saved results, grid count, controls, source dictionary and strongest candidate. The full replay takes much longer and runs in a temporary copy, keeping archived output hashes stable. It executes the source's `K1,K2,A` stages; `--nproc 8` changes worker count, not which configurations are tested. The original K1 program prints its result but does not rewrite the JSON file that the sweep reads. Our runner therefore checks its [live output](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/k1_control_output.txt) and exit status against that pinned file before starting the sweep.

Read the [pinned plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/KDF/PREREG.md), [source executable](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round15/KDF/sweep.py), [complete Stage A result](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/source/liber-primus/analysis/round15/KDF/results_A.json), and [independent checker](experiments/records/public-kdf-seed-stretch/check.py) for exact parameters and values.

records.article:
# Could LP2 be the key to another Cicada text?

The usual question is how to decode Liber Primus. This public test reverses the roles: it treats the **12,956 unsolved LP2 runes as a running key** and asks whether that key reveals a shorter Cicada object. It tests specific objects and rules; it does not directly decrypt LP2.

## Finding

**No tested pairing produced a readable English result.** The best of 40 runs scored **−7.032** on the source's English quadgram scale, below its predeclared **−5.5** advancement bar. The five highest-scoring configurations were also compared with 200 shuffled versions of their target each; none exceeded its corresponding highest shuffle score. A planted message encrypted under the same LP2 key *was* recovered, showing that this decoder can succeed on a constructed example of its assumed mechanism.

![Five target groups and their best English scores, all below the advancement bar.](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/scores.svg)

The graphic shows each target's best run. Higher scores are stronger *for this English model*; the plotted values do not measure an unconditional probability that a puzzle idea is true.

## What entered the test

The source's key stream was the 55 nonempty unsolved LP2 transcription segments concatenated in page order. It tested four versions of that stream: forward, reversed, rune-index Atbash (`28 − index`), and negation modulo 29. Each was used with addition and subtraction in `plaintext = (target + sign × key) mod 29`. The decoder can skip up to three key positions at a time when searching for synchronization.

Five targets entered the completed run:

| Target | Input to decoder | Length actually scored |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| 2012–13 puzzle texts | English text converted to rune indices | first 500 |
| Five solved LP1 pages | their recorded plaintext transliterations converted to rune indices | first 500 |
| PGP message text | English text converted to rune indices | first 500 |
| “AN END” byte sequence | hard-coded bytes reduced modulo 29 | 63 |
| LP2 opening | first 200 runes of LP2 tested against the LP2 key | 200 |

The source proposed a sixth target, the pages 49–51 payload, but did **not** have the payload bytes needed to run it. It therefore ran five targets × four key variants × two signs = **40 decodes**. Negating the key and changing the sign gives the same arithmetic as an unnegated key with the original sign, so some decodes are equivalent; 40 is the run count, not 40 independent hypotheses. Every run starts at key offset zero.

The “AN END” input is the **63-byte hard-coded sequence in the source script**, which labels it a SHA-512 hash. This record preserves that exact input without asserting that the bytes independently authenticate an external artifact. The text-to-rune conversion is likewise the source's conversion, not a lossless representation of the original messages.

## What the control and scores mean

The source first encrypted a known English sentence with the LP2 stream, including deliberate key skips. Its beam decoder recovered the planted transliteration exactly, scoring **−4.413**. A rigid decoder using the right key but no skip search scored **−7.334**. That is a useful positive control for this implementation; it cannot prove that an unknown real message, if present, would be found under every different skip pattern or encoding.

The strongest real-target result was the 2012–13 text under the forward LP2 stream with addition: **−7.032**. For that *selected* run, 200 target-order shuffles reached a highest score of **−6.972**, slightly stronger than the observed result. The null comparison was computed for only the top five selected configurations, and the shuffled controls do not repeat the whole selection process across all target and rule choices. We therefore report the observed absence of a hit under the source's gate, rather than a universal statistical exclusion.

This replay uses the [pinned F-01 executable](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/sweep.py) and [its declared plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/PREREG.md). The source's result prose speaks more broadly than its executed grid in places; the figures above come from the machine-readable run and the independent accounting check.

## Reproduce

Download this experiment's ZIP from the record's download control to inspect the pinned code, input texts, result, and checker. From a Liberpedia repository checkout, run:

```bash
python experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/check.py
python experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/run.py
```

The checker is quick. The complete source replay takes several minutes and runs in a temporary copy, so it leaves the archived result bytes intact. It verifies the complete 40-configuration grid, the positive-control gate, the LP2 rune-stream checksum, the five selected null comparisons, and substantive equality with the pinned source output (excluding elapsed wall time).

The bundled [source results](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/source/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/results.json), [checker](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/check.py), and [figure script](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/plot.py) expose the exact values. The [source README and method notes](experiments/records/public-lp2-as-pad/source/liber-primus/analysis/round16/F-01/PREREG.md) are preserved as evidence of what was proposed, not as broader findings of this replay.

**Remaining scope:** target material other than these five objects, a verified pages 49–51 payload, other key offsets, alternative page boundaries, or using the other objects as key material would require separate tests.

# Multi-rune feedback and autokey

A feedback cipher can derive each new key symbol from earlier symbols. [This published screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round12/C1/RESULTS.md) tested whether LP2 behaves that way when the key depends on the previous two to six runes.

## Finding

**None of the 23,520 source configurations produced a convincing English reading.** The strongest result scored **−6.299**, below the source's required **−5.500**. It came from a **66-rune segment**, not the continuous manuscript: a five-rune plaintext-history XOR rule on the reversed segment, with an all-six seed. The source program successfully recovered all **21 planted cases** at history length three and gave wrong-rule decodes much lower scores.

![The planted control clears the score threshold; the highest-scoring LP2 candidate remains below it.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/scores.svg)

These are English quadgram scores; higher means the transliterated output resembles the training text more closely. The strongest short fragment is still well below the planted English sample. A score by itself would never establish a solution without a coherent continuation.

## How the tested rules work

At each position, the program reads the previous *k* symbols, passes them through one of seven fixed functions, then adds or subtracts the resulting value modulo 29. The seven functions are an index sum, prime-value sum, XOR, prime-of-index-sum, prime-of-prime-sum, last-symbol difference and alternating sum. It tries three kinds of history: the visible ciphertext, the plaintext decoded so far, or the modulo-29 sum of the two. The source also tries both directions of the rune stream and both arithmetic signs.

![A five-rune history is mapped to a key value, then combined with the next ciphertext rune to produce a proposed plaintext rune.](experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/feedback.svg)

The screen covers the **12,956-rune continuous unsolved stream** plus its **55 nonempty source segments**. For ciphertext history, symbols after the first *k* positions do not depend on the initial seed. For plaintext and mixed history, the source tries only the **29 all-equal seeds** `0…0` through `28…28` at each *k*, then keeps the best score. That is a thin slice of the possible **29^k** initial states. In particular, a wrong initial plaintext state need not “lock on” to the correct state later; the source's broader claim that a genuine autokey would necessarily reveal itself under these seeds is not established by this test.

The source's 200 shuffled controls score the raw full stream, while its reported best is selected from thousands of configurations, many on short segments. That shuffle maximum is not a full best-of-grid null. The result is therefore **no supported English reading in the executed grid**, not a statistical exclusion of every feedback cipher.

## Reproduce

Download the experiment ZIP and run from its extracted folder:

```sh
python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/run.py
```

It runs the 21 planted controls before the full sweep, then checks the saved result against the separately archived source output. The independent checker reconstructs the 12,956 source rune indices and **recomputes the winning XOR/plaintext-history decode and score** without calling the source's feedback decoder. For a quick check of the packaged outputs, run `python experiments/records/public-multihistory-feedback/check.py`. The full sweep takes several minutes.

The code, transcription and scoring table are included from [Dukotah/cicada3301 revision f08b20b](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round12/C1), with the repository's license. This record matches that program's executed parameters; it does not claim to rule out other functions, alphabets, seed states or non-English plaintext.

# How much text does a skip-count test need?

One proposed cipher model sometimes advances the key without consuming a manuscript rune. Its exact decoder permits such a skip only when the skipped key position would reproduce the previous ciphertext rune. A decoder can count those extra advances. This [published experiment](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/RESULTS.md) asks when that count can distinguish a **deliberately planted message and its correct key** from random ciphertext paired with random keys. It tests the measuring tool; it does not decode an unsolved page.

## Finding

For the source's exact `keyskip1` decoder, the planted key first clears its **1% two-sided comparison bar at 6,000 runes**. It does not clear the bar at the preceding measured length, 3,600, and it still clears it at 9,000 and 12,956. Thus the observed crossing lies in **(3,600, 6,000]**, on this ten-point length ladder. This is a bound for this plant and this null model, not a universal minimum length or evidence that LP2 uses the modeled cipher.

![The planted correct-key skip count crosses the wrong-key upper-tail threshold at 6,000 runes, then remains above it.](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/crossover.svg)

At 3,600 runes the correct-key path made **94 skips**; the 1% upper-tail threshold of the 300 wrong-key trials was **107**. At 6,000, the correct path made **198**, above a threshold of **176**. The planted plaintext was recovered with at least **99.8% agreement** at every length, so a failed comparison below 6,000 was not caused by a decoder that could not recover its own test message. A reported two-sided value of `0.000` means none of the 300 sampled null trials was as extreme; it is not a zero probability.

## What was tested

The source planted one message at each of **400, 600, 900, 1,200, 1,600, 2,400, 3,600, 6,000, 9,000 and 12,956 runes**, using its fixed skip rule and seed 3301. For each length and decoder mode it compared the correct-key skip count with 300 uniform-random ciphertext and key pairs of the same length. Its criterion required both a two-sided empirical value at or below **0.01** and at least **90%** recovery of the planted message. The two endpoints were checked first: 400 did not separate, while 12,956 did. The source does not cap its doubled-tail statistic at one, so its reported `1.04` at 600 runes is not a probability.

The archive contains **34 reported cells**. Ten lengths were measured for the exact decoder and for a more permissive drift decoder, and a separate ten-length curve planted a `skip_by_two` mechanism. Four additional labels were measured at the 6,000-rune point. Those labels do **not** represent different language corpora in the executable: the plant uses English *Self-Reliance* text for all of them and changes the chosen window with the label. The script also promised an order-preserving shuffle surrogate in its plan, but only the random ciphertext/key null is executed here.

The alternate channels illustrate why a numerical separation cannot stand alone. The permissive drift decoder produces many spurious skips with random keys, so the correct key falls in its **left** tail even at short lengths; that is a different effect from the excess-skip footprint in the exact decoder. The `skip_by_two` plant never reaches the required recovery floor, so its curve cannot establish a crossover for that mechanism. Neither channel should be combined with the exact-channel crossing.

These are **single planted messages per length**, not repeated estimates of how often the method succeeds on arbitrary messages. No LP2 keys were searched, no plaintext language was inferred, and the numerical bound changes if the plant, null, decoder or threshold changes. In particular, this test does not rule out a useful shorter-window statistic or a different skip rule.

## Reproduce

The bundled [result data](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/nskips_crossover.json) retains every discrete null histogram. The [independent checker](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/check.py) recomputes the reported thresholds, tails, crossing and endpoint gate, then compares the replay with the pinned source result. From a Liberpedia checkout:

```bash
python experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/check.py
python experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/run.py
```

The full runner copies the source to a temporary folder. It reuses a null sample when multiple cells call the source with the **same length, decoder mode, seed and 300-trial input rule**; the source would otherwise recompute identical samples. Every resulting cell is checked against the pinned output. For the exact executable, input files and predeclared rules, inspect the [source driver](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/crossover.py), [plan](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/PREREG.md), and [bundled source files](experiments/records/public-nskips-crossover/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L2-nskips-crossover-length/PREREG.md).

# Seven public PRNG constructions against LP2

Could a seeded software random-number generator supply LP2's 29-symbol key stream? This reruns a [published seven-generator screen](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/prng/RESULTS.md) against the first 120 runes of the unsolved text.

## Finding

**No candidate in the executed grid reached the source's required English score.** The replay screened **52,556 decodes**: seven generator implementations, 1,877 fixed seeds, two addition signs and two key directions. The best candidate scored **−6.347**; a candidate needed at least **−5.500** to advance. A planted English message encoded with the source's PHP-style generator scored **−4.155** and was recovered exactly. The same program can therefore find one of its own planted signals under this setup.

These are English quadgram scores: they measure how much a four-letter pattern resembles the training text. **Higher is better**, but even a high score would still require a readable continuation and independent checks before it could count as a solution.

![Three scores on the same scale: planted control clears the bar; the manuscript's best candidate does not.](experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/score.svg)

The winning seed, generator, sign and direction match the archived run. This is evidence about the **specific seeded generators and seed slice below**, not evidence that LP2 uses no PRNG or no stream cipher.

## What was tested

The seven source implementations are PHP-5-style `mt_rand`, .NET-4-style `System.Random`, a simplified single-integer-seeded ISAAC, Blum–Blum–Shub at two fixed moduli, a 32-bit LFSR and a Geffe combination of three LFSRs. Every stream is reduced modulo 29. The key-skip beam searches up to three rejected key symbols at each rune, using the source's English quadgram scorer. Its first-stage ciphertext is exactly the source's 120-rune LP2 prefix, regenerated from the pinned runic transcription.

The 1,877 seeds are **1,828 daily-spaced Unix seconds from 2011–2015 plus 49 fixed number/string-derived seeds**. The source's earlier plan described hourly sampling and an additional rejection reduction; the actual executable and result cover daily sampling and `mod29` only. That difference matters. The test also fixes key offset at zero and does not check other starting positions.

The source calls all seven generators “validated,” but most reference vectors in this script are computed by the same implementation being tested. Self-consistency and a planted decode show that the local program works consistently; they do **not** independently verify exact PHP, .NET or standard ISAAC runtime compatibility. The ISAAC variant expressly uses a simplified seed procedure. We therefore name them as the **source implementations**, not all production runtimes bearing those names.

## Reproduce

Download this experiment's ZIP and run from its extracted folder:

```sh
python experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/run.py
```

The command executes the archived test program, then independently checks the reconstructed ciphertext, case count, control, winning configuration and score against the separately archived original result. It takes several minutes. For a quick integrity check of saved results, run `python experiments/records/public-prng-seed-sweep/check.py`.

The packaged source files are pinned to [Dukotah/cicada3301 revision f08b20b](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/tree/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round16/prng). The original generator code, documented plan and result are retained with this record. The only regenerated source input is `ct.bin`, constructed byte-for-byte from that revision's `krisyotam_runes.txt`; the checker confirms its 12,956 rune indices and SHA-256.

# A public 43-key Vigenère sweep

An archived attempt tried Liber Primus-related words as repeating Vigenère keys. Its [README](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/vigenere/README.md) describes a wordlist; its [output archive](https://github.com/LiberPrimus/Failed-Attempts/blob/d219a8099f8d24e52496e9ee3456ed9980893884/bruteforce/vigenere/vigenere-bruteforce-results.zip) contains **43** rune keys across 58 page files. The archive includes an additional DIVINITY key after the listed words. We take the keys from the archived output, rather than silently reducing the set to the README list.

## Finding

![A fixed-key sweep: 43 keys across 55 rune-bearing unsolved pages, with no 12-rune known-opening match.](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/key-sweep.svg)

All **2,365** rune-bearing key–page prefixes in our LP2-00–55 replay match the beginning of the pinned public output archive. LP2-50 contains only the alphanumeric grid, so its 43 nominal cases have no rune output. None of the 2,365 decoded starts equals any of nine predeclared, 12-rune known-reading openings: **0 of 21,285 comparisons**. A planted MOUNTAIN plaintext encrypts and decrypts correctly with the first source key.

This verifies the public arithmetic for the beginning of each output and rules out **these keys, at page-start phase zero, for these nine exact openings** on our transcription. It does not mean that every wordlist Vigenère attempt has failed. A different key, phase, word-boundary reset, alphabet, page segment, or plaintext beginning is outside this check. The source's “no good result” is an editorial observation, not a numerical language score, so we do not present it as a measured threshold.

## What was done

For every rune position *j* on each page, we computed plaintext index `P[j] = C[j] − K[j mod length(K)] (mod 29)`. Non-rune marks and the number square remain visible but do not advance the key. We kept the GP rune order and the printed page boundaries fixed. The [plan](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/plan.json) pins all 43 rune keys and the public repository revision. The saved [results](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/results.json) give every page/key prefix and its input hash. The independent [check](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/check.py) recomputes those prefixes; when passed the original ZIP, it also checks all 2,365 nine-rune prefixes against the archived headings. The archive uses both `IA` and `IO` for one GP rune, which the checker treats as alternative labels for the *same* symbol.

This is related to the [two known Vigenère keys and nine openings](#/experiments/lp2-known-vigenere-keys), but it is a different fixed source key list and a narrower phase rule. The nine openings are a diagnostic: their absence does not prove that no decoded output contains meaningful text elsewhere.

## Reproduce

From the repository root, run `python experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/check.py`. To verify against the source's archived output, download the ZIP from the pinned GitHub revision, verify its SHA-256 against the [plan](experiments/records/public-wordlist-vigenere/plan.json), then pass it with `--source-archive PATH` to the checker.

# Python 2.7 priority seeds against fixed LP2 openings

**Finding.** None of the **45,975 priority words** in the published [R21-L3 sweep](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/sweep.py) produces any of nine fixed 12-rune known-reading openings at the start of the 55 nonempty pages in LP2-00–55. We checked all four source generator settings—**183,900 generated cases**—under the source's key-skip rule. The closest match reaches five runes.

![No Python 2.7 priority-seed case matches a complete twelve-rune opening; the longest match is five.](experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/prior-front-prefixes.svg)

## What was checked

The source orders 433 proposed 32-bit words, then adds the ±512 neighbourhood around its first 64 words, removing repeated values. That yields **45,975 words** before its later dense-from-zero search. We reconstructed the order from the pinned `seedprior20.json` and checked its SHA-256 digest against the earlier source audit. For each word we used exactly the source's four settings:

| Setting | How the key starts |
| --- | --- |
| `grb5_mod_i386` | One 32-bit seed word; five random bits modulo 29 |
| `grb5_rej_i386` | One 32-bit seed word; reject five-bit values 29–31 |
| `shuffle29_i386` | One 32-bit seed word; repeated shuffled rune alphabet |
| `random29_amd64` | Multiply the word by the source constant into 64 bits; seed with its low and high 32-bit words |

We generated the first **45 key symbols**, enough to allow 12 accepted symbols with up to three rejected symbols between them. A rejected symbol is permitted only if it would have repeated the preceding ciphertext rune. The test searches every valid skip path, without ranking or discarding one because its English score looks poor. It uses the source's subtraction direction, zero starting offset, no Atbash, and the same nine predeclared openings used in other site experiments.

## What the result means

| Best opening prefix per case | Generated cases |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 rune | 115,884 |
| 2 runes | 64,488 |
| 3 runes | 3,409 |
| 4 runes | 108 |
| 5 runes | 11 |
| All 12 runes | **0** |

There are **183,356 different first-45-symbol streams** among the 183,900 generated cases. The counts above are settings and seeds tested, not separate solving ideas. The useful conclusion is limited: *this priority seed grid cannot produce any of these nine exact openings at those page starts under the stated skip rule.* Other plaintext openings, later positions, further seeds and other key rules are outside the result.

R21-L3 originally screened **884,000** word-and-setting cases on LP2-00 with an English-language panel. This record does **not** reproduce that language-panel claim: its model inputs are unavailable in the pinned source. The fixed-opening criterion here is independent of that panel and asks a narrower, directly checkable question.

## Reproduce

From the repository root:

```bash
python experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/run.py
python experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/check.py
python experiments/records/py27-prior-front-opening-cribs/plot.py --check
```

The record bundles the pinned source seed list and Python 2.7 generator under their MIT license. `results.json` gives each setting's prefix counts and a digest over all 183,900 case results. The separate checker rebuilds the whole grid, uses its own exact path-state search, checks 400 small cases against brute tree search, verifies a reference MT19937 output vector, and recovers planted openings with and without a forced skipped key symbol.

## Finding

The pinned source reports a sweep of **884,000 seed words** across four Python 2.7-style keystream configurations. It saved **95 candidates** that passed its first screen. We can check those saved rows: they divide into **21, 25, 24 and 25** by configuration, and none clears the source's final score bar of **7.6342**. Their highest final score is **6.248**. The underlying 884,000 first-stage scores were *not* saved, so the sweep total and the claim that no omitted candidate passed remain source-reported rather than independently recomputed here.

The source's planted-key control passes **4/4** in its saved output, but it begins at the **full 240-rune evaluation**. The actual sweep first applies a **120-rune, narrower-beam screen** and promotes a word only when that score reaches **5.0**. The control never calls this screening function. It therefore shows the final evaluator can recognize its own planted text; it does **not** measure whether the first gate would pass that text. The exact model file needed to try the gate is missing from the pinned public repository, as are three of the corpus files required to rebuild it.

![The actual sweep has a first screening gate that the planted control skips.](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/screen-control-gap.svg)

This is a **source-method audit**, not a new negative decryption result. The saved rows support a narrower statement: *among the 95 recorded promotions, no candidate met the published final score threshold.* They do not establish a measured false-negative rate for Stage A or a ruling on Python-derived keystreams in general.

## What was in the source sweep

| Rune reducer / seed map | Screened, reported | Saved promotions | Best saved final score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `getrandbits(5) % 29`, one word | 288,000 | 21 | 6.089 |
| Reject `getrandbits(5)` values 29–31, one word | 216,000 | 25 | 5.260 |
| Repeated shuffle of 29 values, one word | 186,000 | 24 | 6.248 |
| `int(random() × 29)`, two-word seed map | 194,000 | 25 | 5.341 |

The source orders **433 proposed seed words**, expands neighborhoods around its top 64, and deduplicates them to **45,975** words before a dense count from zero. We independently reconstructed that ordering from the pinned seed-prior file. The recorded screen counts are each larger than 45,975, consistent with the source's statement that it completed this front in every configuration. Because only promoted rows were persisted, their actual first-stage scores and the rest of each scan cannot be audited from the receipts alone.

There is a small but concrete reporting error: the prose says **71 of 95** promotions had both recovery fields equal to 1.000. The pinned rows contain **67**. This does not change the observed zero final-bar clearances, but it illustrates why the rows matter more than summary prose.

## Scope and how to retest

The source decodes the **first 120 runes of LP2-00** for screening and the **first 240** for its final gate. Its key is a seed word passed through one of the four specified reducer/map combinations. The searched fractions of each nominal 2³²-word space are roughly **0.004–0.007%**. The two-word map is a deterministic 32-bit-to-64-bit fold used by the source, not an enumeration of all 64-bit Python hash values. Other seeds, other reducers, other cipher relations and plaintexts outside the source's scoring panel remain untested here.

The [pinned sweep code](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/sweep.py), [planted control](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/poscontrol.py), [saved rows](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/reducers_sweep.jsonl) and [aggregate](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/out_reducers.json) are included with hashes. Reconcile them without the absent model using:

```text
python experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/run.py --check
python experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/check.py
python experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/plot.py --check
```

To establish the broader negative, first restore the original `panel.npz` or its exact training inputs, then run the **complete planted control through Stage A and Stage B**. Persist each screened word's first-stage score or a verifiable checkpoint before repeating the bounded sweep. The original [preregistration](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source/liber-primus/analysis/round21/L3-py27-reducers-plus-64bit-map/PREREG.md) describes that intended bound; the [source manifest](experiments/records/py27-reducer-sweep-source-audit/source-manifest.json) identifies the bytes audited here.

# How far does the QuagMirror draft run?

**Result.** The pinned public script processes the first **six runes of LP2-00**, then deliberately stops. An independent replay obtains the same index streams and the transliteration **DCBWJO**. That is a match to the draft program's output, not a reading of the page. The code does not run its proposed method across a complete word or page.

The idea combines an autokey calculation with one of nine handwritten 29-symbol substitution tables. At each position, Möbius values associated with the position and a prime-derived totient choose the table. Previous cipher and output symbols feed the next autokey calculation. The first two positions contain explicit overrides in the source. Those choices are retained here; silently removing them would replay a different method.

![A five-row diagram traces the six cipher indices through the autokey indices, selected mirror tables, output indices and Latin fragments.](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/six-rune-trace.svg)

| Stage | Six values |
| --- | --- |
| Archived LP2-00 rune indices | 15, 8, 18, 3, 6, 19 |
| Autokey indices | 15, 28, 2, 10, 3, 14 |
| Output indices | 23, 5, 17, 7, 11, 3 |
| Latin fragments | D C B W J O |

The replay checks the source's first six input indices against this site's LP2-00 transcription. It stores all nine permutation tables and every fixed choice in the [plan](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/plan.json), then calculates each row in the [result](experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/results.json). The tables are permutations, but that property alone does not make the output intelligible or prove an encryption mechanism.

This is a **WIP source-version replay**. The repository contains several changing scripts; it would be misleading to combine their rules into one historical "QuagMirror" result. The particular file [Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py at pinned commit 88ef1e60](https://github.com/sgroveman/cicada3301_lp/blob/88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307/Solving%20Attempts/Mobius_AT_QuagMirror.py) has SHA-256 `e317878190994910afbbdc5707a66af73a684b29abdd9d7e443563aba9d15a66`. Its `break` after six processed positions is part of the code, so this record cannot test its remaining page output, any later revisions or proposed thematic keywords. A complete candidate needs one frozen version, a declared rule for every position, full output and an untouched-text check.

Run `python experiments/records/quagmirror-six-rune-replay/run.py --check` from the repository root. Python's standard library suffices. The saved plan and results make this exact six-position variant available offline without shipping the source discussion or changing its unfinished state.

# Three QuagMirror drafts beyond the six-rune example

The [six-rune draft](#/experiments/quagmirror-six-rune-replay) is one of four scripts in the same [pinned public repository](https://github.com/sgroveman/cicada3301_lp/tree/88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307/Solving%20Attempts). We ran the other three **as written**, including their fixed debug stops and handwritten mirror tables. All start from the same 729 source rune indices covering LP2-00–02. The indices match Liberpedia's page transcription after treating the two printed forms of the J rune as the same alphabet position.

## Finding

The scripts process **49, 153 and 500 positions** respectively. Each produces short English-like fragments mixed with unreadable text. None processes its whole 729-rune input, supplies a planted recovery control, or checks a reading on held-out text. Reproducing these outputs establishes what the drafts actually do; it does not establish a plaintext for LP2.

![The original script stops after 153 runes, version 4 after 49, and the WIP script after 500; page boundaries occur after 262 and 528.](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/coverage.svg)

| Script | Positions | Beginning of its output |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Original | 153 | `DIUINITY WITHIN HAUING BOTH IHING...` |
| Version 4 | 49 | `DIUINITY WITHIN PRAY FOR ANY CORRUPTIBLE...` |
| WIP | 500 | `DIUINITH WITHIN EUEN DIATH OSW...` |

These are **three different drafts**, not three confirmations of one decryption. Their rules and stopping points differ. Version 4 contains a pass-through at source index 17 that uses `continue` before the loop counter advances. Its nominal `index >= 48` debug stop therefore occurs after **49 input positions**. We retain that behavior; silently changing it would create another method. The [complete outputs and numeric streams](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/results.json) are saved so a promising fragment can be read in context rather than selected in isolation.

## What the replay checks

Each script contains nine 29-symbol substitution tables, a hard-coded 729-index ciphertext, a numerical recurrence, and a Latin-fragment mapping. The [checker](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/check.py) confirms that the tables are permutations, the source ciphertext matches the 729 runes on LP2-00–02, the printed numeric rows have the stated lengths, and the printed final text follows from those numeric outputs and the script's own spacing marks. This independently checks the **input and output trace**; it is not an independent proof that the recurrence recovers meaningful plaintext.

The first fragments may look deliberate. Assessing them requires the full output, a fixed method for every rune, a criterion chosen before seeing the result, and a positive control showing that the program can recover a known message made with its proposed cipher. The source drafts provide no such control. The longer WIP output is valuable evidence of how the apparent opening continues under the same code, but it does not by itself validate or refute every QuagMirror-style method.

## Reproduce

From a Liberpedia checkout with Python 3 and SymPy installed:

```bash
python experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/check.py
python experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/run.py
```

The runner executes the three bundled [pinned scripts](experiments/records/quagmirror-variant-continuations/source/OG_quag_mirror.py), extracts their complete printed output tables, and compares the results with the saved file. Their source revision is `88ef1e60b0738b8b28db96bc9dc44dc4da8dd307`; the record lists every file hash. No word choice, table, or stop point is adjusted during the replay.

# Older random generators against fixed LP2 openings

**Finding.** We rebuilt the [R26-A source grid](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round26/A/sweep.py) of Perl, TeX and Python 2.7 keystreams and asked whether any could begin an unsolved LP2 page with one of nine known 12-rune readings. Across **24,231 generated key cases**, each checked under the source's two skip rules, **none matched a complete opening**. The closest matched four runes.

![The longest opening matched four of twelve runes; no source-defined configuration matched all twelve.](experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/opening-prefixes.svg)

This is a **fixed-opening check**, not a rerun of R26-A's English-scoring test. The source tested a 333-rune page with a language panel and reported an interim result. Here the question is narrower and exact: *could a named plaintext opening be structurally produced at a page start?*

## What went into the check

The source's ordered dictionary has **347 entries**: puzzle numbers, the first 200 primes, sparse dates, prime sums of solved-text words and those words as Python 2 string seeds. Its **400 integers from 0 to 399** add a small baseline. Some entries repeat values under another label. We preserved the complete executable generator grid:

| Source generator | Generated key cases | Two skip rules |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Eight Perl `rand` reductions | 5,696 | 11,392 |
| Four TeX random generators | 2,848 | 5,696 |
| Three Python 2.7 reductions, seven offsets each | 15,687 | 31,374 |
| **Total** | **24,231** | **48,462** |

Those cases contain **19,986 different first-100-symbol streams**; repeated seeds and equivalent settings make some duplicate prefixes. The case count describes the source grid, not 24,231 independent ideas or keys.

Perl and TeX accept integer seeds here; Python 2.7 also accepts the 35 word seeds. Python 2.7 uses the source's 64-bit seeding path and offset list **0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 13**. The source's `count_decodes()` announces 49,302 rows because it counts all 347 dictionary entries for Perl and TeX. Its actual loop skips their 35 string seeds, removing **840** rows. We counted the executable loop, not the announced estimate.

For every key stream, we tested the first 12 runes on all **55 nonempty pages in LP2-00–55**—LP2-50 is blank—against the same **nine predeclared 12-rune openings** used in the site's other fixed-opening experiments. We kept the source's subtraction direction, no Atbash, and zero starting offset. The `exact` rule may reject up to three key symbols before an accepted rune; each rejected symbol must otherwise repeat the previous ciphertext rune. The `pair` rule may reject up to eight in pairs; the first symbol of each rejected pair must make that repeat. Every feasible path is considered, without an English-score beam that could prune one.

Only the first **100 key symbols** are needed to test a 12-rune opening under the larger eight-rejection bound. Generating a longer forward stream would leave those symbols unchanged. This shortens the computation without truncating any possible 12-rune path.

## Result and meaning

| Longest feasible prefix among the nine openings and 55 pages | Configurations |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 rune | 30,680 |
| 2 runes | 16,909 |
| 3 runes | 842 |
| 4 runes | 31 |
| All 12 runes | **0** |

A one-rune match says little: each key is compared with many page-and-opening pairs. The decisive fact for this specific test is that **no complete 12-rune opening is possible anywhere in the declared grid**. That does *not* show that these generators cannot encrypt LP2. The unknown pages might begin with other words, use another offset or direction, reset the key, or follow a different transition rule. The original R26-A language-panel outcome is a separate claim.

## Reproduce and inspect

From the repository root:

```bash
python experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/run.py
python experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/check.py
python experiments/records/r26-derived-generators-opening-cribs/plot.py --check
```

The ordered seed manifest and original generator modules are bundled with the record under the source's MIT license. The results file records each generator/preset distribution, every complete match (there were none), and a digest over all 48,462 configuration results. An independent checker regenerates the full grid with a separate path-state implementation, compares that implementation with brute tree search on 400 small cases, verifies generator vectors against independent arithmetic or a captured Python 2.7 vector, and recovers planted no-skip and forced-skip openings. Current site rune transcriptions and the published reading cribs are the target inputs; changing either requires a new run.

records.article:
## Finding

**A straightforward rail-fence reading does not stand out in this bounded test.** Across LP2-00–55, the best of nine rail counts matched **70** words in a fixed English list. The same nine-way search on page-rotated controls had a median of **78** matches; **195 of 199** controls matched at least 70. The unchanged rune order matched 57. These are dictionary matches, not a translation.

![The best rail-fence word count is below the median of the alignment controls.](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/comparison.svg)

## The proposal and the actual test

[TheronEagle's public rail-fence script](https://github.com/TheronEagle/liber-primus-research/blob/a6c5d13f7591030367daace993c887af20a5e0ab/experiments/2026-09-24/rail_fence_test.py) decrypts each page using two through ten rails and scores the resulting letters as words in a dictionary. Its saved result names two rails as the highest scorer. The repository points to an absolute local path for its word list and another for its transcription; neither file is part of that repository. Its numeric result therefore cannot be exactly replayed from its published checkout.

Here the input is Liberpedia's pinned LP2-00–55 rune text: **12,956 runes** arranged into **2,776 visible word slots**. As in the source code, a hyphen ends a slot; line-break marks and punctuation do not. The [fixed 369,652-word list](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/lexicon.txt) is derived from the [Unlicense English-words repository](https://github.com/dwyl/english-words/blob/20f5cc9b3f0ccc8ce45d814c532b7c2031bba31c/words_alpha.txt), with the exact transform and source hash in [SOURCE.txt](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/SOURCE.txt). A decoded slot counts only when its exact GP Latin transliteration is in that list. The denominator includes short slots that cannot score, so the counts should be compared only under this same scoring rule.

| Reading | Matched slots |
| --- | ---: |
| Printed order, no rail transform | 57 |
| Two, four, or nine rails | 70 each |
| Median of 199 control maxima | 78 |

Each control rotates the rune stream of *each page* by a seeded, nonzero offset, keeps its visible word lengths, tests all nine rail counts, and retains the best score. The page's rune inventory and contiguous ciphertext order remain intact; the rotation changes the alignment with word slots. This comparison asks whether the printed alignment of the proposed rail reading is better than the same method applied at other alignments. It is not a model of how Cicada composed the manuscript. The saved control maximum scores range from **67 to 90**. The complete nine-rail counts and all 199 control maxima are in [results.json](experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/results.json).

## What this does and does not exclude

The decoder was checked two ways: the main script encrypts an actual solved-page rune sequence and recovers it at each rail count, while the separate checker recomputes all manuscript outputs through a different index permutation. This rules out a broken rail inverse as the explanation for the ordinary score.

The test covers **only** conventional page-by-page rail-fence decryption with two through ten rails, this word segmentation, this GP transliteration and this fixed dictionary. It says nothing about keyed columns, a rail count outside the range, combining pages, moving word boundaries, a preceding substitution layer, or a non-English plaintext. In particular, the source repository's wider statement that all transpositions are ruled out does not follow from these nine cases.

To reproduce offline, use the experiment ZIP and run `python experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/run.py --check`, followed by `python experiments/records/rail-fence-visible-words/check.py`. Both need Python 3 and the archived source files; no network call is made during the run.

records.article:
## Result

**The thirteen pages with large red initials do not have unusual spacing under this uniform-page comparison.** Their largest consecutive run is two pages; a random set of thirteen pages has a run of at least two **96.8%** of the time. Their first and last marked pages are LP2-00 and LP2-57, so their span is the full release; that cannot be unusually short. The variance of the twelve internal gaps is **12.85**; **32.8%** of 100,000 random sets have at least that much variance. This tests page placement, not whether the artwork carries a message.

![The published total-red selection, corrected large-initial pages, and two planted spacing controls on the same 58-page axis.](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/page-order.svg)

The top row reproduces the [published total-red page list](https://github.com/Dukotah/cicada3301/blob/f08b20b632d91209ddbaa747e8e2f23df0c78ba1/liber-primus/analysis/round22/D-illustration-dropcap/RESULTS.md). Its highlighted LP2-07 and LP2-53 are [small red text, not large initials](#/wiki/red-initials). The corrected row has thirteen pages. LP2-03 and LP2-33 each have two large initials; this test deliberately reduces each page to a single yes/no mark.

## What was compared

The [image audit](research/red-initials-audit.csv) freezes which of the 58 LP2 pages contain a large red connected shape. The comparison draws **100,000** uniform 13-page subsets without replacement. It asks whether the actual pages have unusually variable internal gaps, a short overall span, a long run of adjacent pages, or an unusually compressible 58-bit presence string. Span and run probabilities are also counted exactly over all **3,155,581,562,280** possible 13-page subsets. Five declared tail directions are considered together; none approaches the adjusted threshold.

| Measure | Observed | Comparison result |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Variance of the 12 gaps | 12.85 | 32.8% of random sets are at least as variable; 67.4% are no more variable. |
| Span, last minus first | 57 pages | All 13-page sets have a span of 57 or less. |
| Longest consecutive run | 2 pages | 96.8% of random sets have a run of at least two. |
| zlib size of the packed page bits | 16 bytes | 99,977 of 100,000 random sets also occupy 16 bytes; this score has almost no resolving power here. |

The comparison deliberately assumes every 13-page placement is equally likely. It is a baseline for visible spacing, **not** a model of how the manuscript was composed. A rule based on section boundaries, the identities of the initials, or two initials on one page is outside it.

## Can these checks detect a planted pattern?

The lower two rows of the figure are fixed controls with the same thirteen marks. Approximately even spacing gives a very small gap-variance tail in the sampled comparison, while thirteen consecutive marks give an exact short-span and long-run probability of **46 / 3,155,581,562,280**. But both controls have low gap variance: that one statistic cannot tell even spacing from a single compact block. The evenly spaced control still compresses to 16 bytes, so the compression check would miss that visible regularity. These limitations matter when interpreting the ordinary manuscript result.

The earlier study also tested red-pixel centroids and an initial-rune string. Those are **not** reproduced here: its total-red mask includes two pages without initials, its centroids include all red marks rather than only the large shapes, and several pages have a second or later initial. A corrected identity or position test needs explicit annotation of each large initial before scoring.

## Reproduce

Download the [original JPEGs](downloads/original-images.zip) if you want to repeat the image classification itself. With Python 3 and Pillow, NumPy and OpenCV installed, run `python scripts/audit_red_initials.py > research/red-initials-audit.csv`. The page-order test then needs only Python's standard library:

```text
python experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/run.py --check
python experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/check.py
python experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/plot.py
```

The [plan](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/plan.json) pins the image-audit table and analysis rules. [Results](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/results.json) retain every observed statistic, tail count and planted control; the [separate check](experiments/records/red-initial-presence-order/check.json) verifies the exact arithmetic and repeats the gap comparison with another random stream. This is an exploratory correction after the source classification error was seen, not a preregistered test of all ways the manuscript could encode information.
